questions.stem: CT shows normal trachea, but marked swelling involves the lips, tongue, and arytenoids. Which airway division is primarily affected?
options: Entire airway from mouth to bronchioles
questions.explanation: The upper airway includes the nose, mouth, pharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and cricoid cartilage; the lower airway starts at the trachea.

questions.stem: A mass narrows the left mainstem bronchus 3 cm below the carina. Which airway division is involved?
questions.explanation: The lower airway begins at the trachea and includes the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli.

questions.stem: Micrognathia and cleft palate result from abnormal craniofacial development. Which embryologic structures contribute importantly to airway formation?
questions.explanation: Airway structures derive from pharyngeal arches 1–4 and 6; first-arch problems affect the mandible and palate.

questions.stem: A tracheostomy bypasses which two protective functions normally provided by the nose? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The nose humidifies, filters, and adds resistance to airflow. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, and phonation at the larynx.

questions.stem: For effective topical anesthesia before nasal intubation, which sensory pathways must be blocked?
questions.explanation: Nasal sensation comes from the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) branches of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.stem: Brisk epistaxis occurs during nasal intubation. Which arterial sources are most relevant?
questions.explanation: The nose is supplied by branches of the maxillary, ophthalmic, and facial arteries; vasoconstrictors reduce bleeding.

questions.stem: Loss of pharyngeal tone during anesthesia allows the tongue to obstruct the airway. Which structure commonly contributes to the same collapse?
questions.explanation: General anesthesia reduces pharyngeal dilator tone. The tongue and soft palate can then fall posteriorly and narrow the upper airway, whereas the hard palate and trachea are rigid structures that do not collapse in this way.

questions.stem: Which two congenital conditions are strongly associated with upper-airway obstruction? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Pierre Robin (micrognathia, glossoptosis) and Down syndrome (macroglossia, small airway) predispose to obstruction.

questions.stem: Which palate description is anatomically correct?
options: The hard palate is anterior and fixed
The hard palate is posterior and mobile
The soft palate is anterior and fixed
questions.explanation: The hard palate is the fixed anterior two-thirds; the soft palate is the mobile posterior third.

questions.stem: The opening between the faucial arches with the tonsils between them is called the:
questions.explanation: The fauces is the opening from the oral cavity into the oropharynx.

questions.stem: Why does visibility of the fauces matter during Mallampati assessment?
options: It helps distinguish lower classes from class III
questions.explanation: Seeing the fauces is part of the Mallampati classification, distinguishing lower classes from class III and IV.

questions.stem: A pharyngeal mass lies around C5–C6. Which segment is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx sits at C1, the oropharynx at C2–C3, and the hypopharynx at C5–C6.

questions.stem: Regurgitated gastric contents reach the pharynx during deep anesthesia. Which structure normally serves as the main barrier at the top of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The upper esophageal sphincter prevents regurgitation into the pharynx, and anesthetics relax it.

questions.stem: During awake fiberoptic intubation, touching the epiglottis still triggers cough despite glossopharyngeal blockade. Which sensory nerve was most likely missed?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The internal SLN provides sensation above the cords, including the epiglottis; it needs its own block or topicalization.

questions.stem: Which nerve provides motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies motor innervation to nearly all intrinsic laryngeal muscles. The key exception is the cricothyroid, which is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: After neck surgery, the vocal cords still move but cannot tense normally. Which muscle is most likely impaired?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid tenses and lengthens the vocal cords and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Injury can therefore impair pitch or cord tension while other recurrent-laryngeal-nerve-mediated movements remain intact.

questions.stem: After thyroidectomy, a patient has a breathy voice and coughs with liquids but no severe airway obstruction. Which nerve injury best fits?
questions.explanation: Unilateral RLN injury causes hoarseness and aspiration; bilateral injury can cause respiratory distress.

questions.stem: Immediately after thyroidectomy, severe stridor develops and both vocal cords are immobile near midline. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Bilateral RLN injury leaves both cords near midline, obstructing the airway, and often requires reintubation.

questions.stem: Which two cranial nerves provide the major sensory and motor innervation of the pharynx and larynx? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves supply the pharynx and larynx. The phrenic, facial, trigeminal, and hypoglossal nerves do not.

questions.stem: The adult larynx spans approximately which vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The larynx extends from about C3 to C6.

questions.stem: The thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottic cartilages belong to which group?
questions.explanation: The thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottis are the three single (unpaired) laryngeal cartilages.

questions.stem: An arytenoid is dislocated after traumatic intubation. How is the arytenoid classified?
questions.explanation: The arytenoid, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages are paired.

questions.stem: Which two functions are primarily performed by the larynx? (Select 2)
options: Protection of the lower airway from aspiration
Participation in gag and cough reflexes
questions.explanation: The larynx protects the lower airway from aspiration and enables gag and cough reflexes, along with phonation and patency.

questions.stem: In a cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate emergency, the membrane palpated between thyroid and cricoid cartilages is the:
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane connects the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and is the site for emergency cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: When identifying the cricothyroid membrane by landmarks, which anterior thyroid-cartilage feature is commonly palpated first?
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage laminae fuse anteriorly at the thyroid notch.

questions.stem: Bleeding from the supraglottic larynx is traced to a branch of the superior thyroid artery. Which branch is involved?
questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal artery, from the superior thyroid artery, supplies the supraglottic larynx.

questions.stem: Bleeding from the infraglottic larynx is traced to a branch of the inferior thyroid artery. Which vessel is involved?
questions.explanation: The inferior laryngeal artery, from the inferior thyroid artery, supplies the infraglottic larynx.

questions.stem: Which muscle group closes the glottis and adjusts vocal-cord tension?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles control cord tension and glottic opening and closure.

questions.stem: Impaired elevation and positioning of the larynx during swallowing most directly indicates dysfunction of which muscle group?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic laryngeal muscles position the larynx during phonation, breathing, and swallowing.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy, the depression between the tongue base and epiglottis is the:
questions.explanation: The vallecula lies between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis.

questions.stem: With a Macintosh blade, where should the tip be placed to elevate the epiglottis indirectly?
questions.explanation: A Macintosh blade is placed in the vallecula. Lifting tensions the hyoepiglottic ligament and indirectly elevates the epiglottis, unlike a straight blade that directly lifts the epiglottis.

questions.stem: An ETT tip lies just below the cricoid cartilage. Which airway segment has it entered?
questions.explanation: The trachea begins at the cricoid cartilage and ends at the carina.

questions.stem: Approximately how long is the adult trachea from cricoid to carina?
questions.explanation: The adult trachea is about 10–20 cm long, so a tube can easily be advanced too far.

questions.stem: About how many C-shaped cartilaginous rings are present in the adult trachea?
questions.explanation: The trachea contains 16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings.

questions.stem: Which laryngeal cartilage forms a complete ring and serves as a fixed airway landmark?
questions.explanation: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.

questions.stem: During coughing, which posterior tracheal structure contracts to narrow the lumen and relaxes to permit esophageal expansion?
questions.explanation: The trachealis muscle aids cough and lets the esophagus expand during swallowing.

questions.stem: At approximately what airway diameter is cartilage no longer present in the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: Cartilage disappears at about 0.6–0.8 mm, so bronchiolar patency depends on smooth muscle tone.

questions.stem: Which mainstem-bronchus angle best explains the tendency of a deeply advanced ETT to enter the right side?
questions.explanation: The right mainstem leaves the trachea at about 25–30°, making it more in line with the trachea than the left.

questions.stem: Why does inadvertent mainstem intubation usually enter the right bronchus?
options: The right bronchus is more vertical and straighter
questions.explanation: The right mainstem bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertically aligned with the trachea than the left. A deeply advanced endotracheal tube therefore preferentially enters the right mainstem.

questions.stem: Why can a right-sided double-lumen tube obstruct the right upper lobe more easily?
options: The right upper-lobe bronchus originates only about 2.5 cm below the carina
It originates about 10 cm below the carina
It is narrower than the left upper-lobe bronchus
It arises from the left mainstem
questions.explanation: The right upper lobe bronchus arises about 2.5 cm from the carina, so a deep cuff can occlude it.

questions.stem: Airway manipulation triggers parasympathetic bronchoconstriction. Which nerve carries this input to the tracheobronchial tree?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the trachea and bronchi.

questions.stem: An ETT is advanced too deeply and causes violent coughing with sympathetic activation. Which structure is most likely being stimulated?
questions.explanation: The carina is highly sensitive; contact causes coughing, bronchospasm, and hemodynamic responses.

questions.stem: During which stage of lung development does the lung bud first appear?
questions.explanation: The laryngotracheal groove and lung bud form in the embryonic stage.

questions.stem: By approximately what developmental time are bronchopulmonary segments recognizable?
questions.explanation: Bronchopulmonary segments appear by day 42 of gestation.

questions.stem: A 25-week premature infant needs exogenous surfactant. During which developmental stage does endogenous surfactant production begin?
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes begin producing surfactant during the canalicular stage, although production is initially limited and increases later in gestation. This helps explain the high respiratory-distress risk of extreme prematurity.

questions.stem: Why is gas exchange severely limited in an infant born at 24 weeks?
options: The alveolar-capillary barrier is still developing
questions.explanation: The blood-gas barrier begins forming around week 26, so earlier infants have limited gas exchange.

questions.stem: When does postnatal alveolar development substantially approach the mature pattern described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Alveolar development continues until about 3 years of age and beyond with growth.

questions.stem: During which developmental stage does extensive branching produce terminal bronchioles?
questions.explanation: The pseudoglandular stage (weeks 6–16) features rapid branching.

questions.stem: After interscalene block, ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis occurs. Which nerve and roots were affected?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) innervates the diaphragm and is often blocked by interscalene injections.

questions.stem: Which two embryologic structures contribute substantially to diaphragm formation? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum and pleuroperitoneal folds, along with the dorsal esophageal mesentery and body wall.

questions.stem: A newborn has severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest. Which developmental defect best explains the physiology?
questions.explanation: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia permits abdominal viscera to enter the thorax, compressing the developing lung and causing pulmonary hypoplasia. Bowel sounds in the chest with a scaphoid abdomen strongly point to this defect.

questions.stem: Which germ-layer pairing correctly explains the origin of lower-airway epithelium versus its supporting connective tissues?
questions.explanation: The lower respiratory tract develops from endodermal epithelium and surrounding mesoderm.

questions.stem: Which growth-factor pair is most important for fetal airway branching and pulmonary vascular development?
questions.explanation: FGF-10 drives airway branching and VEGF drives pulmonary vascular development.

questions.stem: During swallowing, which structure most directly deflects material away from the glottic opening?
questions.explanation: The epiglottis covers the glottis during swallowing.

questions.stem: The folds extending from the epiglottis to the arytenoids form the lateral borders of the laryngeal inlet. What are they?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglottic folds lie lateral to the laryngeal inlet.

questions.stem: A foreign body lodges lateral to the aryepiglottic fold. Which recess is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The piriform recesses lie lateral to the aryepiglottic folds.

questions.stem: After thyroid surgery, a singer has preserved conversational speech but can no longer reach high notes. Which muscle is most likely weak?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid (external SLN) tenses the cords; injury causes loss of high pitch.

questions.stem: Bilateral injury leaves the vocal cords unable to abduct. Which muscle normally provides the only active vocal-cord abduction?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor; losing it bilaterally causes obstruction.

questions.stem: During laryngospasm, which intrinsic muscles are most responsible for forceful vocal-cord adduction?
questions.explanation: The thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid (RLN) adduct the cords; the cricothyroid (SLN) tenses them. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor.

questions.stem: A patient has limited mouth opening and a short neck before thyroidectomy. What is the main purpose of the airway assessment?
options: Identify likely challenges and build a patient-specific airway plan
Replace the need for backup equipment
questions.explanation: Airway evaluation identifies potential challenges so you can build a specific plan with backups.

questions.stem: Mallampati is I, but thyromental distance is 4 cm and neck extension is limited. Which interpretation is best?
options: Trust Mallampati because it is most reliable
Combine predictors because no single test is sufficiently reliable
questions.explanation: Individual airway tests have low sensitivity and specificity, so findings must be combined.

questions.stem: Which four components of airway management should be assessed before anesthesia? (Select 4)
options: Direct or video laryngoscopy with intubation
questions.explanation: Airway planning should separately consider the ability to provide bag-mask ventilation, perform laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation, place a supraglottic airway, and obtain emergency front-of-neck access. Failure in one domain does not guarantee failure in the others.

questions.stem: Which two historical clues should raise the strongest concern for prior airway difficulty? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Clues to prior airway difficulty include chipped teeth and unexpected ICU admission, as well as sore throat and remembered difficult intubation.

questions.stem: A department performs 5,000 tracheal intubations each year. Based on the cited incidence, approximately how many difficult intubations should be expected?
questions.explanation: Difficult tracheal intubation occurs in about 1.5–8.5% of cases.

questions.stem: Among 5,000 intubations, approximately how many complete failures would be expected from a 0.3%–0.5% failure rate?
questions.explanation: Failed tracheal intubation occurs in about 0.3–0.5% of cases, varying by setting.

questions.stem: A student performs Mallampati with the patient supine and phonating. Which correction makes the exam valid?
options: Patient seated upright, tongue protruded, without phonation
questions.explanation: The modified Mallampati is done seated upright, mouth open, tongue protruded, without phonation.

questions.stem: The soft palate, full uvula, fauces, and tonsillar pillars are visible. Which Mallampati class is present?
questions.explanation: Class I shows the soft palate, uvula, fauces, and pillars or tonsils.

questions.stem: Only the soft palate and base of the uvula are visible. Which Mallampati class and implication best fit?
options: Class III with increased difficult-laryngoscopy risk
Class IV with no visible soft palate
questions.explanation: Class III shows the soft palate and base of the uvula and is associated with difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Only the hard palate is visible during Mallampati assessment. Which class is this?
questions.explanation: Class IV shows only the hard palate.

questions.stem: Which Mallampati classes are associated with increased risk of difficult laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: Mallampati classes III and IV are associated with a higher likelihood of difficult laryngoscopy because progressively fewer oropharyngeal structures are visible. Mallampati is only one predictor and should be combined with other airway findings.

questions.stem: The epiglottis is visible during routine mouth opening before laryngoscopy. How is this unusual finding classified?
options: A common marker of difficult airway
questions.explanation: Mallampati class zero means the epiglottis is visible, found in about 1.2% of patients.

questions.stem: Why should the patient avoid saying 'ah' during a modified Mallampati exam?
options: Phonation can falsely improve the oropharyngeal view
questions.explanation: Phonation elevates the soft palate and can improve visualization of pharyngeal structures, making the airway appear more favorable than it is under standardized conditions. The modified Mallampati examination is therefore performed without saying 'ah.'

questions.stem: Which three additional measurements improve airway prediction when combined with Mallampati? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Combine MMC with TMD, interincisor gap, and neck circumference.

questions.stem: A prior airway note documents 'Cormack-Lehane IIa.' What type of information does this grade convey?
questions.explanation: The Cormack-Lehane system grades the laryngoscopic view.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy shows the entire glottic opening. Which Cormack-Lehane grade is this?
questions.explanation: Grade I is a full view of the glottis including the anterior commissure.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy shows the posterior cords and arytenoids but not the full glottis. Which grade best fits?
questions.explanation: Grade IIa shows a partial view of the cords with the posterior cartilages.

questions.stem: The epiglottis is visible, but no part of the glottic opening can be seen. Which Cormack-Lehane grade is this?
questions.explanation: Grade III shows the epiglottis only, with no glottis. Grade IV shows neither epiglottis nor glottis.

questions.stem: Neither the epiglottis nor glottis is visible during direct laryngoscopy. Which Cormack-Lehane grade is this?
questions.explanation: Grade IV shows neither the epiglottis nor the glottis.

questions.stem: Which Cormack-Lehane views are generally associated with easier tracheal intubation?
questions.explanation: Grades I and IIa are generally easier; grade IIb and higher are associated with difficulty.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy shows roughly half of the vocal cords in a typical adult. Which grade and frequency best fit?
options: Grade II, the most common view
Grade I, the most common view
Grade III, the most common view
questions.explanation: Grade II, seeing part of the cords, is the most common view.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy reveals no useful glottic view. Which next step best changes airway geometry rather than repeating the same failed attempt?
options: Repeat blindly with the same blade
Apply cricoid pressure and repeat unchanged
Pass a bougie through visible cords
questions.explanation: A grade IV view means nothing is visible. Reposition, readjust, or move to VL rather than repeating the same attempt.

questions.stem: How should thyromental distance be measured correctly?
options: Hyoid to mentum with head neutral
Sternal notch to mentum with mouth closed
Thyroid notch to mentum with head extended and mouth closed
Thyroid notch to mentum with head flexed and mouth open
questions.explanation: TMD is measured from the thyroid notch to the mentum with the head extended and mouth closed.

questions.stem: A thyromental distance of 4 cm should be interpreted how?
options: Short; normal is at least about 6 cm
questions.explanation: A normal TMD is at least 6 cm; a short TMD predicts a poor view.

questions.stem: An unusually long thyromental distance of 10 cm may reflect which laryngeal position that can also complicate direct laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: A TMD over 9 cm may indicate a caudally placed larynx that is hard to visualize.

questions.stem: A patient with retrognathia has a thyromental distance of 4 cm. Why does this anatomy increase laryngoscopy difficulty?
options: There is inadequate mandibular space to displace the tongue
questions.explanation: A small mandibular space prevents tongue displacement, blocking the glottic view.

questions.stem: Which two conditions are associated with abnormal thyromental distance? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Abnormal TMD is associated with mandibular hypoplasia and OSA, and a short TMD suggests an anterior larynx.

questions.stem: Which three distances form the 3-3-2 airway assessment?
options: Mouth opening, neck extension, and Mallampati
questions.explanation: The 3-3-2 rule measures mouth opening, mentum to hyoid, and hyoid to thyroid notch.

questions.stem: Fewer than two fingerbreadths between the hyoid and thyroid notch suggests what airway geometry?
questions.explanation: Less than 2 fingerbreadths suggests an anterior larynx.

questions.stem: More than two fingerbreadths between the mandibular-neck junction and thyroid notch suggests what laryngeal position?
questions.explanation: More than 2 suggests a low larynx.

questions.stem: A patient with TMJ disease opens only 2.5 cm. Which airway consequence is most likely?
options: Difficult intubation because blade and tube access are limited
questions.explanation: An interincisor opening below about 3 cm limits room to insert and manipulate a laryngoscope and pass an endotracheal tube. Adequate mouth opening is therefore important even when other airway measurements are reassuring.

questions.stem: Why does a two-fingerbreadth mouth opening make direct laryngoscopy difficult?
options: The blade and tube may not have adequate passage
questions.explanation: Limited mouth opening prevents the blade and tube from passing.

questions.stem: Large protruding upper incisors most directly create which pair of problems during laryngoscopy?
options: Dental injury risk and impaired line of sight
Lower aspiration risk and easier tube passage
questions.explanation: Prominent upper incisors increase dental injury risk and narrow the line of sight.

questions.stem: How should sternomental distance be measured?
options: Thyroid notch to mentum with mouth open
Hyoid to mentum with head neutral
Sternal notch to hyoid with head flexed
Sternal notch to mentum with the head extended
questions.explanation: SMD is measured from the sternal notch to the mentum with the head extended and mouth closed.

questions.stem: A sternomental distance of 11 cm in full extension predicts what?
questions.explanation: An SMD under 12.5 cm is associated with difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Sternomental distance increases only 3 cm from neutral to full extension. How should that change be interpreted?
options: A change under about 5 cm suggests limited mobility and greater difficulty
Change in SMD is not predictive
questions.explanation: A change of less than 5 cm from neutral to extension suggests difficult laryngoscopy; this patient changed only 3 cm.

questions.stem: Approximately how much atlanto-occipital extension is expected in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: The AO joint normally allows up to 35° of extension.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has only 18° of atlanto-occipital extension. What does this imply for airway management?
questions.explanation: Restricted atlanto-occipital extension limits alignment and positioning needed for direct laryngoscopy. An extension of only 18° is below the cited threshold and should increase concern for a difficult laryngoscopic view.

questions.stem: From adolescence to older age, approximately how much can cervical flexion-extension decrease?
questions.explanation: Range of motion decreases about 20% with age.

questions.stem: Which two conditions commonly reduce atlanto-occipital mobility? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Degenerative cervical disease and cervical trauma limit atlantooccipital mobility, as does Down syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient in a halo fixator has essentially no cervical motion. Which intubation approaches best minimize the need for neck movement?
questions.explanation: When cervical mobility is limited, VL or flexible endoscopy avoids the need for neck extension.

questions.stem: During airway assessment, a patient can open widely but cannot advance the lower incisors beyond the upper incisors. Which function is the upper lip bite test primarily assessing?
options: Mandibular protrusion and temporomandibular joint mobility
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test assesses mandibular protrusion and TMJ mobility.

questions.stem: A patient cannot bring the lower incisors into contact with the upper lip despite adequate mouth opening. How should this ULBT finding change your airway assessment?
options: Class B; laryngoscopy is likely easy
Class C; mask ventilation is predicted to be easy
Class C; difficult laryngoscopy is more likely
Class A; laryngoscopy is likely easy
questions.explanation: The upper lip bite test reflects mandibular protrusion and temporomandibular-joint mobility. Inability to bring the lower incisors to the upper lip is class C and indicates restricted protrusion, increasing the likelihood of difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: During the upper lip bite test, the lower incisors extend above the vermilion border of the upper lip. Which class is present?
questions.explanation: Class A means the lower incisors bite above the vermilion border.

questions.stem: An edentulous patient has a reassuring Mallampati score, but the upper lip bite test cannot be interpreted reliably. What is the main limitation?
options: The maneuver depends on the lower incisors
Edentulous patients usually have reduced cervical motion
The maneuver isolates neck extension rather than jaw movement
Edentulous status itself predicts a difficult laryngoscopy
questions.explanation: The ULBT relies on lower incisors, so it is less reliable in edentulous patients or when used alone.

questions.stem: Two patients have identical Mallampati scores. One has a 46-cm neck circumference. What does that additional finding imply?
options: It is reassuring if mouth opening is normal
It has no independent airway relevance
It adds concern for airway difficulty
questions.explanation: A neck circumference over 43 cm suggests airway difficulty.

questions.stem: Which TWO findings should increase concern for difficult direct laryngoscopy despite otherwise normal vital signs? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A prominent overbite and a high, narrow palate suggest difficult laryngoscopy, as does a stiff mandibular space. A TMD above 6 cm is reassuring.

questions.stem: A patient has several predictors of difficult laryngoscopy. A trainee argues that planned videolaryngoscopy makes the preoperative airway exam unnecessary. Which response is BEST?
options: Videolaryngoscopy replaces assessment in elective cases
Videolaryngoscopy changes device choice but does not replace airway assessment
Videolaryngoscopy makes an airway exam unnecessary if oxygenation is normal
Only Mallampati becomes irrelevant; thyromental distance remains mandatory
questions.explanation: VL has changed the predictive value of traditional tests, but assessment still guides planning and backups.

questions.stem: A clinician measures from the mandible-neck junction to the thyroid notch rather than from the mentum. Which airway measurement is being obtained?
questions.explanation: The modified hyomental distance runs from the mandible-neck junction to the thyroid notch.

questions.stem: Mallampati is class II, but thyromental distance is short and neck extension is limited. What is the best interpretation?
options: The reassuring Mallampati overrides the other findings
The tests conflict, so none should influence planning
All three tests measure the same anatomic limitation
Combining the findings is more predictive than relying on one test
questions.explanation: Mallampati evaluates only one component of airway anatomy. A short thyromental distance and limited neck extension add independent concerns, so the combined assessment is more informative than allowing a reassuring single test to override the others.

questions.stem: Which FOUR findings increase the likelihood that bag-mask ventilation will be difficult? (Select 4)
options: Young age with normal body mass index
questions.explanation: Predictors include facial hair, edentulous, obesity, elderly, snoring/OSA, Mallampati III/IV.

questions.stem: Which patient has the strongest age-related contribution to difficult mask ventilation?
questions.explanation: Age over 55 is associated with difficult mask ventilation because of reduced tissue elasticity.

questions.stem: A patient has a BMI of 34, beard, and normal Mallampati score. Which finding still warrants planning for more difficult mask ventilation?
options: BMI does not matter until it exceeds 45
Only underweight patients have BMI-related mask difficulty
questions.explanation: Obesity (BMI over 30) is a predictor of difficult mask ventilation.

questions.stem: After induction, mask ventilation produces minimal chest rise, a weak ETCO2 trace, and SpO2 falls to 91%. What is the best interpretation?
options: Ventilation is adequate because saturation remains above 85%
Ventilation is adequate because any ETCO2 trace is sufficient
The pattern is most consistent with pulse oximeter artifact
Mask ventilation is inadequate and should be escalated
questions.explanation: Signs of inadequate BMV include poor chest movement, low or absent ETCO2, poor breath sounds, and SpO2 below 92%.

questions.stem: Before induction, you deliberately assess external appearance, the 3-3-2 relationship, Mallampati class, obstruction, and neck mobility. Which structured assessment are you using?
questions.explanation: The LEMON-type approach covers external look, 3-3-2, Mallampati, obstruction or obesity, and neck mobility. SHORT predicts difficult cric.

questions.stem: Which FOUR findings make supraglottic airway placement or ventilation through it less reliable? (Select 4)
options: Low pulmonary compliance or stiff lungs
questions.explanation: SGA difficulty comes from limited opening, obstruction, distortion, and stiff lungs.

questions.stem: A patient with prior neck surgery, radiation, and a large anterior neck tumor may require emergency front-of-neck access. Which mnemonic specifically highlights predictors of a difficult cricothyrotomy?
questions.explanation: SHORT predicts difficult cricothyrotomy: Surgery, Hematoma, Obesity, Radiation, Tumor.

questions.stem: A patient has prior neck radiation and a large neck mass, making rescue front-of-neck access potentially difficult. What is the most useful step BEFORE induction?
options: Avoid discussing the neck because it may increase anxiety
Perform prophylactic tracheostomy in every such patient
Wait to identify landmarks until a rescue is needed
Identify and mark the cricothyroid membrane
questions.explanation: Prior radiation and a neck mass can make emergency front-of-neck access difficult. Identifying and marking the cricothyroid membrane before induction reduces delay if an invasive rescue airway becomes necessary.

questions.stem: A cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate emergency occurs in a patient with prior neck radiation and obesity. How should those factors affect the decision to perform cricothyrotomy?
options: They increase technical difficulty but do not preclude emergency access
A neck mass makes cricothyrotomy absolutely contraindicated
questions.explanation: There are no absolute contraindications to emergency cricothyrotomy when the patient cannot be oxygenated.

questions.stem: A trauma patient requires airway management and has midline cervical tenderness. Which imaging study best evaluates a suspected cervical spine fracture?
questions.explanation: CT is the gold standard for cervical spine fractures.

questions.stem: In a patient with BMI 55, the cricothyroid membrane cannot be palpated reliably before induction. Which bedside tool is most useful for localization?
questions.explanation: POCUS can identify the cricothyroid membrane in obese patients.

questions.stem: Preoperative airway ultrasound shows markedly increased pretracheal soft-tissue thickness. Which problem should this finding make you anticipate?
questions.explanation: Increased pretracheal soft tissue thickness predicts difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A department performs 44,000 general anesthetics annually. Using a major airway complication rate of about 1 in 22,000, what is the expected annual number?
questions.explanation: NAP4 found about 1 major airway complication per 22,000 anesthetics: 44,000 ÷ 22,000 = 2.

questions.stem: If airway-related death occurs at roughly 1 per 180,000 anesthetics, what number would be expected across 180,000 anesthetics?
questions.explanation: NAP4 reported about 1 airway death per 180,000 anesthetics.

questions.stem: An obstetric service performs 600 general anesthetics. If cannot-intubate, cannot-ventilate occurs about once per 300 obstetric anesthetics, how many events would be expected?
questions.explanation: The obstetric CICV incidence is about 1 in 300: 600 ÷ 300 = 2.

questions.stem: The lecture gives a CICV incidence of about 1 in 300 in obstetrics versus 1 in 2,250 outside obstetrics. Approximately how do the rates compare?
options: Obstetric CICV is about 2 times higher
Obstetric CICV is about 7.5 times lower
Obstetric CICV is about 7.5 times higher
questions.explanation: 2,250 ÷ 300 = 7.5, so obstetric CICV is about 7.5 times more common.

questions.stem: A service performs 2,000 inductions. If difficult facemask ventilation occurs in about 0.9%–7.8%, which range is most plausible?
questions.explanation: Difficult facemask ventilation occurs in about 0.9–7.8% of patients.

questions.stem: A service performs 2,000 supraglottic airway insertions. With a failure rate of about 0.19%–1.1%, which range is most plausible?
questions.explanation: SAD failure occurs in about 0.19–1.1% of cases.

questions.stem: Which TWO intraoperative conditions are specifically associated with supraglottic airway failure? (Select 2)
options: Normal dentition with a good seal
questions.explanation: SAD failure is linked to poor seal and table rotation, as well as dentition problems, male sex, and high BMI.

questions.stem: Compared with the operating room, adverse airway events causing death or brain damage are reported to be how much more likely in the emergency department or intensive care unit?
questions.explanation: Adverse airway events are 30–60x more likely in ED/ICU.

questions.stem: When planning prehospital airway rescue training, what upper-end emergency cricothyrotomy rate should the team recognize from the lecture data?
questions.explanation: Emergency cricothyrotomy rates in prehospital settings can reach 11%.

questions.stem: A patient with pharyngolaryngeal disease is scheduled for biopsy. Which approximate difficult-intubation rate best reflects the lecture data for this population?
questions.explanation: Difficult intubation occurred in about 28% of patients with pharyngolaryngeal disease.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy unexpectedly fails despite a normal bedside airway exam. Flexible evaluation reveals bulky tissue at the tongue base. Which occult problem best explains the mismatch?
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsil hyperplasia can cause unanticipated difficult or failed airways despite a normal exam.

questions.stem: Which TWO symptoms should increase suspicion for lingual tonsil hyperplasia in a patient whose routine airway exam is otherwise reassuring? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsil hyperplasia presents with sore throat and globus sensation, along with dysphagia, snoring, and OSA.

questions.stem: For a routine elective induction in a healthy adult, which sequence best preserves oxygenation while confirming the ability to ventilate before paralysis?
options: Neuromuscular blocker → propofol → laryngoscopy → BMV → preoxygenation
Preoxygenation → neuromuscular blocker → propofol → BMV → laryngoscopy
Preoxygenation → propofol → confirm BMV → neuromuscular blocker → laryngoscopy
Propofol → neuromuscular blocker → preoxygenation → laryngoscopy → BMV
questions.explanation: The standard sequence is preoxygenation, induction agent, confirming mask ventilation, NMB, then laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, oxygen progressively replaces nitrogen within the functional residual capacity. What process is occurring?
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation is also described as nitrogen washout or denitrogenation.

questions.stem: A healthy, fully preoxygenated adult with normal functional residual capacity becomes apneic after induction. Approximately how long may oxygen saturation remain acceptable under ideal conditions?
questions.explanation: Up to 8 minutes of safe apnea in healthy patients.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, expired oxygen reaches 75% with a tight mask and 100% inspired oxygen. Using the target taught in this airway lecture, how should this be interpreted?
options: Adequate; this lecture lists a goal above 70%
questions.explanation: This lecture lists an expired O2 goal above 70%; the Phases lecture used about 90%.

questions.stem: A cooperative elective patient has normal lungs and no urgency. Which preoxygenation method best maximizes oxygen reserve before induction?
options: Loose mask with room air for 5 minutes
Tight seal with 100% oxygen for 3–5 minutes
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min for 1 minute
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation needs a good seal, high-flow 100% O2, and large tidal breaths for 3–5 minutes.

questions.stem: Urgent induction is required and there is not enough time for 3–5 minutes of tidal breathing. Which alternative provides effective rapid preoxygenation?
options: Twenty tidal breaths on room air
questions.explanation: Eight vital capacity breaths in 60 seconds is an accepted alternative to 3–5 minutes of tidal breathing.

questions.stem: Two intubation attempts have failed and SpO2 is falling, but the patient can still potentially be ventilated by mask. What should be prioritized FIRST?
options: Proceed directly to videolaryngoscopy without ventilating
questions.explanation: When oxygenation is deteriorating after failed intubation, restoring ventilation takes priority over repeated intubation attempts. If bag-mask ventilation remains possible, it is the fastest immediate means of reoxygenating the patient.

questions.stem: A trainee presses the mask downward and ventilation worsens because the mandible is displaced posteriorly. Which correction is most appropriate?
options: Loosen the mask and accept a leak
Use the chin as a thumb fulcrum
Use a C-E grip while lifting the jaw into the mask
questions.explanation: The C-E grip lifts the mandible into the mask; pressing down pushes the jaw back and worsens obstruction.

questions.stem: Which FOUR findings together provide evidence that bag-mask ventilation is effective? (Select 4)
options: Condensation or fog in the mask
questions.explanation: Look for chest rise, fog, and ETCO2.

questions.stem: One-handed mask ventilation is marginal in a bearded patient with obstructive sleep apnea and a thick neck. Which next maneuver is most likely to improve ventilation?
options: Use a smaller mask and simply increase oxygen flow
Insert an oral airway and use a two-hand mask technique
Increase inspiratory pressure while keeping the same one-hand grip
Switch to a smaller mask regardless of fit
questions.explanation: A two-hand mask technique improves both the mask seal and mandibular advancement; an oral airway can relieve tongue-related obstruction. These maneuvers directly address common causes of inadequate bag-mask ventilation in an obese patient with obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.stem: Immediately after induction, mask ventilation produces no chest rise. Before moving to a supraglottic airway or invasive rescue, what should be done FIRST?
questions.explanation: Repositioning is the first step in BMV escalation, before adjuncts or devices.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation remains inadequate after induction. Which escalation order is most appropriate?
options: Reposition → OPA → two-hand seal → SGA or ETT → cricothyrotomy if oxygenation still fails
questions.explanation: Escalate from repositioning to an OPA, a two-hand seal, then an SGA or ETT, and cric if all fail.

questions.stem: A bearded, obese patient cannot be ventilated effectively with a one-hand mask grip. What is the main advantage of switching to a two-person bag-mask technique?
options: One provider can maintain a two-handed seal and jaw thrust while the other ventilates
It allows faster ventilation regardless of seal
questions.explanation: Two-person BMV lets one provider use both hands for the seal and jaw thrust while the other bags.

questions.stem: An obese, edentulous patient with a nasogastric tube is predicted to be difficult to mask ventilate. Which THREE steps can improve the chance of effective BMV? (Select 3)
options: Leave dentures in when they improve the mask seal
questions.explanation: Ramping, keeping dentures in when they help the seal, removing an NG tube, and preparing alternatives all improve BMV.

questions.stem: A term parturient and a patient with BMI 50 both desaturate rapidly during apnea despite similar preoxygenation. Which shared physiologic change best explains this?
questions.explanation: Obesity and pregnancy reduce FRC, shrinking the oxygen reserve.

questions.stem: During apnea, oxygen continues to move from the pharynx into the alveoli even without diaphragmatic movement. What creates this inward flow?
options: Residual negative pressure from the final breath
Oxygen uptake exceeds carbon dioxide return, creating a pressure gradient
questions.explanation: During apnea, oxygen continues to be removed rapidly from the alveoli while much less carbon dioxide enters them because most CO2 is buffered in blood and tissues. The resulting subatmospheric alveolar pressure draws oxygen down a patent airway even without active ventilation.

questions.stem: During apnea, oxygen uptake continues but relatively little carbon dioxide returns to the alveoli. Approximately how much CO2 enters the alveoli each minute?
questions.explanation: Only ~8–20 mL/min CO2 enters alveoli.

questions.stem: During RSI in an obese patient expected to desaturate rapidly, you add standard nasal-cannula apneic oxygenation. Which flow rate best matches the lecture approach?
questions.explanation: Standard nasal cannula at 15 L/min is used for apneic oxygenation.

questions.stem: Apneic oxygenation is running at the planned flow, but SpO2 falls rapidly while the tongue completely obstructs the pharynx. Which prerequisite has failed?
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation depends on an open path from the oxygen source to the alveoli. Complete pharyngeal obstruction prevents oxygen from reaching the lungs, so saturation can fall despite an adequate nasal-cannula flow rate.

questions.stem: After prolonged apneic oxygenation, SpO2 remains 95% but pH is 7.15 with rising PaCO2. Which principle best explains the discordance?
options: CO2 builds up without ventilation, causing acidosis
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation can continue supplying oxygen without removing carbon dioxide. SpO2 may therefore remain acceptable while PaCO2 rises and respiratory acidosis progresses, which is why oxygenation is not equivalent to ventilation.

questions.stem: A standard nasal cannula is left at 15 L/min for an extended period during repeated airway attempts. Which complication becomes increasingly relevant?
questions.explanation: High-flow oxygen should be short-term to avoid airway mucosal damage.

questions.stem: Which patient is most likely to gain meaningful extra safe-apnea time from apneic oxygenation?
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation is most useful in obese patients or during prolonged attempts.

questions.stem: After induction, mask ventilation remains poor with a snoring obstructive sound despite jaw thrust. What is the most appropriate next maneuver?
options: Insert an OPA to relieve tongue obstruction
Insert an NPA to confirm tracheal placement
Wait to insert an OPA until after intubation
Insert an NPA to prevent laryngospasm
questions.explanation: An oral airway relieves tongue obstruction when BMV is inadequate.

questions.stem: A trainee documents 'VL performed' but not whether the trachea was intubated. Which distinction is most accurate?
options: DL places the tube; VL visualizes
questions.explanation: DL and VL describe how the larynx is visualized; TI is passing the tube through the cords.

questions.stem: In a child with a long floppy epiglottis, a Miller blade is chosen because it is designed to do what?
options: At the base of the tongue
questions.explanation: The straight Miller blade lifts the epiglottis directly.

questions.stem: A Macintosh blade is correctly seated in the vallecula. Through which mechanism should the epiglottis elevate?
questions.explanation: The Mac blade lifts the epiglottis indirectly via the hyoepiglottic ligament.

questions.stem: During direct laryngoscopy, which maneuver most directly risks dental injury and should be avoided?
options: Levering the blade against the teeth
Sweeping the tongue to the left side
questions.explanation: Using the maxillary teeth as a fulcrum concentrates force on the incisors and can cause dental trauma. The laryngoscope should be lifted along its handle rather than rocked backward against the teeth.

questions.stem: The glottic view improves when thyroid cartilage is displaced backward, cephalad, and rightward. Which maneuver is being used?
questions.explanation: BURP is backward, upward, and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage to improve the view.

questions.stem: An assistant applying BURP asks what 'upward' means anatomically. Which direction is correct?
questions.explanation: In BURP, upward means cephalad, toward the head.

questions.stem: The distal ETT opening becomes partially opposed to the tracheal wall, yet ventilation remains possible. Which tube feature explains this?
questions.explanation: The Murphy eye provides a distal opening if the tip is obstructed.

questions.stem: Two hours into a case, cuff pressure is 40 cmH2O with no leak. What is the best response?
options: Leave it, since higher pressure prevents aspiration
questions.explanation: Cuff pressure should not exceed 25 cmH2O to avoid tracheal mucosal injury.

questions.stem: During nitrous oxide anesthesia, ETT cuff pressure rises from 22 to 38 cmH2O despite no added air. What is the likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide diffuses into an air-filled endotracheal-tube cuff faster than nitrogen diffuses out. Cuff volume and pressure can therefore rise during nitrous oxide anesthesia even when no additional air is injected.

questions.stem: You need routine oral ETTs for average-sized adult female and male patients. Which size pairing is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Typical adult sizes are 6.5–7.0 mm for women and 7.0–7.5 mm for men.

questions.stem: A 6.0 ETT is used instead of a 7.0. Using Poiseuille's relationship, what change in resistance is most likely?
questions.explanation: For laminar flow, resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Even a modest decrease in endotracheal-tube diameter therefore produces a large increase in resistance; the cited 7-to-6 comparison is roughly an 85% increase.

questions.stem: A surgeon needs maximal exposure for excision of a small vocal-cord lesion. Which tube best balances a narrow external diameter with adult length?
questions.explanation: Microlaryngeal tubes are small-diameter, full-length tubes for laryngeal surgery.

questions.stem: For a long prone spine case with head rotation, which ETT design best reduces the risk of kinking?
questions.explanation: Armored tubes contain a wire coil that resists kinking.

questions.stem: A lobectomy requires reliable lung isolation and independent ventilation. Which airway device is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Double-lumen tubes isolate and ventilate each lung separately.

questions.stem: During thoracic surgery, continuous visualization of tube position is desired without repeatedly inserting a bronchoscope. Which tube provides this capability?
options: A double-lumen tube with a bronchial cuff
questions.explanation: The VivaSight ETT has an integrated camera.

questions.stem: Which population has traditionally been managed with uncuffed ETTs rather than standard cuffed adult tubes?
questions.explanation: Uncuffed ETTs have traditionally been used in neonates and infants.

questions.stem: A towel flexes the lower cervical spine while the atlantooccipital joint is extended. Which position is created?
questions.explanation: The sniffing position combines neck flexion with atlantooccipital extension.

questions.stem: A patient with obesity and poor airway alignment needs positioning optimized before laryngoscopy. Which intervention is most useful?
questions.explanation: Use pillows, towels, or ramping.

questions.stem: With a Macintosh blade, where should initial oral insertion occur so the tongue can be swept left?
options: Into the right side of the mouth
Into the left side of the mouth
questions.explanation: The curved blade enters on the right and sweeps the tongue to the left.

questions.stem: A trainee begins levering the laryngoscope against the maxillary teeth. Which lifting vector should replace that movement?
questions.explanation: Lift along the handle at about 45° forward without levering on the teeth.

questions.stem: Before nasotracheal intubation, both nostrils appear similar externally. What is the best bedside method to choose the side of insertion?
options: Use the right nostril by default
Use the left nostril by default
questions.explanation: Testing airflow through each nostril helps choose the more patent side.

questions.stem: Before nasal intubation, which topical therapy most directly reduces mucosal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Topical vasoconstrictors such as phenylephrine or oxymetazoline reduce nasal bleeding.

questions.stem: During nasal tube advancement, how should the bevel be oriented to reduce turbinate trauma?
questions.explanation: Bevel away from midline reduces turbinate avulsion risk.

questions.stem: A nasal ETT repeatedly meets resistance when directed superiorly. Which path should be used instead?
options: Along the floor of the nose
Toward the top of the nose
questions.explanation: The nasal ETT should advance along the floor of the nose below the inferior turbinate.

questions.stem: During nasal advancement, at what approximate depth should the tube tip enter the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The nasal ETT typically reaches the oropharynx at about 14–16 cm.

questions.stem: Magill forceps are needed to direct a nasal ETT into the glottis. Where should the tube be grasped to avoid cuff damage?
questions.explanation: Grasp the tube proximal to the cuff to avoid tearing it.

questions.stem: A dental case requires nasal intubation in a patient with restricted oral access. Which THREE techniques remain appropriate? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Nasal intubation can be blind, VL-assisted, or fiberoptic.

questions.stem: A patient with a wired mandible has severely limited oral access. In which situation is nasotracheal intubation especially useful?
options: When oral intubation is difficult or impossible
When the patient has a basilar skull fracture
questions.explanation: Nasotracheal intubation is useful when oral access is limited, such as mandibular fractures.

questions.stem: A patient will remain intubated for 6 hours. Which cuff design minimizes focal tracheal mucosal pressure?
questions.explanation: Standard ETTs use high-volume, low-pressure cuffs that spread pressure over more tracheal surface.

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects at the proximal ETT connection. Which component interfaces directly with the circuit?
questions.explanation: The 15-mm adapter connects the ETT to the circuit.

questions.stem: Post-intubation chest radiography shows the ETT tip only 1 cm above the carina. Where should it ideally be positioned?
questions.explanation: The ETT tip should sit mid-trachea, above the carina, to avoid endobronchial migration.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation, laryngoscopy, and emergency front-of-neck access are each potentially difficult in the same patient. Which term encompasses this situation?
options: Failed airway after one attempt at DL
A Mallampati IV airway found on the preoperative exam
questions.explanation: A difficult airway involves trouble with mask ventilation, SGA, laryngoscopy, intubation, extubation, or invasive access.

questions.stem: After multiple failed intubation attempts, mask ventilation is also inadequate and SpO2 is 80%. Which term best describes the situation?
options: A difficult airway that needs a bougie on the first pass
Failed airway: unable to intubate or ventilate after multiple attempts
questions.explanation: A failed airway is the inability to intubate or ventilate after multiple attempts and requires immediate rescue.

questions.stem: Which FOUR approaches form the core airway-management strategies available when escalating care? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The four are mask ventilation, SGA, tracheal intubation, and invasive airway.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings represent distinct mechanisms of airway difficulty rather than reassuring features? (Select 3)
options: An expanding neck hematoma after thyroidectomy
Severe hypoxia or hypotension limiting safe apnea time
questions.explanation: Difficult airway causes are anatomic, pathophysiologic, traumatic, and physiologic, including shock and hypoxia that shorten safe apnea time.

questions.stem: Which TWO findings most strongly indicate that mask ventilation is becoming difficult? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Difficult ventilation shows as mask leak and gastric insufflation, along with poor chest rise, SpO2 under 92%, and the need for two hands or adjuncts.

questions.stem: An SGA leaks at only 12 cmH2O despite repositioning. What does this imply about ventilation through the device?
options: A normal seal for most patients
questions.explanation: A leak pressure under 15 cmH2O suggests difficult supraglottic airway ventilation.

questions.stem: Before choosing any airway device for a minor procedure, what is the first question in the Airway Approach Algorithm?
options: Can the patient be intubated awake?
questions.explanation: The first question is whether airway management is needed at all.

questions.stem: Which FOUR items, in addition to deciding whether airway management is needed, belong to the Airway Approach Algorithm? (Select 4)
options: Is the patient at risk of aspiration?
Is DL/VL and intubation expected to be difficult?
Is the patient at risk of rapid desaturation?
questions.explanation: Five questions: necessity, difficulty, supralaryngeal ventilation, aspiration risk, rapid desaturation.

questions.stem: Pre-induction assessment identifies aspiration risk, anticipated difficult intubation, and rapid desaturation risk. What should happen next?
questions.explanation: Concern on any question prompts alternative plans.

questions.stem: A predicted difficult airway is identified in preop. When should the rescue strategy and backups be finalized?
questions.explanation: A predicted difficult airway should have a primary plan, rescue options, equipment, and help identified before induction. Waiting until the first failure wastes time after oxygen reserve and airway control may already be deteriorating.

questions.stem: A department is standardizing its difficult-airway response. Which major guideline frameworks are most commonly referenced?
questions.explanation: The ASA algorithm and DAS guidelines are the major difficult airway algorithms.

questions.stem: Why do major difficult-airway algorithms rely heavily on expert consensus rather than large randomized trials?
options: Outcomes vary too much between countries
Events are too rare for RCTs
questions.explanation: Critical airway events are rare, so randomized trials are difficult, and algorithms rely on consensus.

questions.stem: A known difficult-airway patient with severe OSA requires awake intubation. How should opioids be handled during sedation?
options: Avoid or minimize them to protect spontaneous ventilation
Use them because they preserve ventilatory drive
Use them as the required core of awake sedation
questions.explanation: With a difficult airway, avoid opioids that can cause apnea and loss of the airway before it is secured.

questions.stem: A patient with a large mediastinal mass and stridor may lose airway patency after induction. Which technique best preserves the safety margin?
options: Use deep neuromuscular blockade for a still field
Use controlled ventilation with deep paralysis
Prioritize opioid analgesia for comfort during laryngoscopy
Preserve spontaneous ventilation, such as with awake intubation
questions.explanation: In difficult airways, preserving spontaneous ventilation keeps a safety margin if the airway cannot be secured.

questions.stem: Why is meticulous preoxygenation especially important when difficult laryngoscopy and prolonged attempts are anticipated?
options: It increases tidal volume after induction
It increases the oxygen reservoir in FRC and extends safe apnea time
It stores CO2 to restore respiratory drive
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation replaces nitrogen in the FRC with oxygen, and apneic oxygenation prolongs time to desaturation.

questions.stem: You are rebuilding a difficult-airway cart. Which FOUR components should be treated as core rather than optional? (Select 4)
options: Several laryngoscope blade types and sizes
questions.explanation: Core components include laryngoscopy tools, alternative devices, confirmation tools, and airway anesthesia.

questions.stem: A cart already contains standard blades, tubes, oral airways, suction, bougies, and SGAs. Which addition is useful but considered optional rather than core in this lecture?
questions.explanation: VL and flexible scopes are optional additions to the core difficult airway cart.

questions.stem: A patient is predicted to be difficult to intubate and difficult to rescue if spontaneous breathing is lost. Which strategy best preserves safety?
options: Routine IV induction and direct laryngoscopy
Rapid-sequence induction because the stomach may be full
Deep sedation without securing the airway
Awake intubation while maintaining spontaneous ventilation
questions.explanation: Awake intubation is used when difficult airway is anticipated and spontaneous ventilation must be maintained.

questions.stem: Which FOUR findings independently strengthen the indication for awake intubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Indications include prior difficulty, unstable C-spine, tumors, trauma, burns, OSA, and limited opening.

questions.stem: Which TWO physiologic advantages are preserved by awake intubation compared with inducing general anesthesia first? (Select 2)
options: Removes the need for topical anesthesia
questions.explanation: Awake intubation preserves spontaneous breathing and muscle tone, as well as airway reflexes. It takes more time and preparation.

questions.stem: Secretions are obscuring topicalization during awake intubation. Which medication choice most directly addresses that problem?
questions.explanation: Antisialagogues dry secretions.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient receives lidocaine by nebulizer, spray, and regional airway blocks. What total dose ceiling should guide the combined plan?
questions.explanation: Estimate a maximum of about 4–5 mg/kg IV equivalent, or 280–350 mg for 70 kg, counting every route.

questions.stem: During awake intubation, sedation deepens and upper-airway tone begins to disappear. Which principle has been violated?
options: Avoid deep sedation that may collapse the airway
Use deep sedation to prevent coughing
questions.explanation: Deep sedation may cause airway collapse.

questions.stem: If light sedation is needed for awake intubation, which group contains agents commonly used for that purpose?
questions.explanation: Optional sedation includes dexmedetomidine, midazolam, or fentanyl.

questions.stem: A full-stomach patient with GERD needs awake intubation. Which THREE drugs best target aspiration risk reduction before airway manipulation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A nonparticulate antacid, a gastrokinetic, and an H2 antagonist reduce aspiration risk and harm.

questions.stem: During topicalization, the posterior one-third of the tongue and oropharynx remain sensitive. Which nerve has not been adequately anesthetized?
questions.explanation: CN IX supplies posterior tongue, oropharynx, and upper larynx.

questions.stem: A patient coughs vigorously when the trachea below the vocal cords is stimulated despite good supraglottic anesthesia. Which nerve distribution remains intact?
questions.explanation: The RLN supplies below the cords and trachea.

questions.stem: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue remains sensitive during awake airway preparation. Which sensory nerve must be addressed?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve (V3) supplies the anterior tongue.

questions.stem: For awake nasal intubation, which group of nerves most directly supplies the nasal mucosa requiring topical anesthesia?
options: Anterior ethmoidal, nasopalatine, and sphenopalatine nerves
questions.explanation: Nasal anesthesia targets trigeminal branches.

questions.stem: You choose nebulized lidocaine for awake airway topicalization. Which preparation best matches the lecture protocol?
options: 20 mL of 2% lidocaine with no vasoconstrictor added
4–10 mL of 4% lidocaine plus 1 mL of 1% phenylephrine
questions.explanation: Nebulizer: 4–10 mL 4% lidocaine + 1 mL 1% phenylephrine.

questions.stem: A case starts in 5 minutes, but you are relying on nebulized airway topicalization alone. What practical limitation matters most?
questions.explanation: Nebulization requires 10–20 minutes.

questions.stem: After topical benzocaine, a patient becomes cyanotic despite a high PaO2. Which complication should be suspected first?
questions.explanation: Benzocaine carries a risk of methemoglobinemia.

questions.stem: A tongue blade coated with 5% lidocaine paste is held against the posterior tongue to anesthetize the vallecular region. Which technique is this?
options: Lidocaine jelly on the ETT cuff
questions.explanation: It anesthetizes the posterior tongue, vallecula, and epiglottis.

questions.stem: For a glossopharyngeal nerve block, where should the needle be placed?
options: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal block is at the base of the palatoglossal arch.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal block, aspiration returns blood before injection. What is the safest immediate response?
options: Stop and switch to general anesthesia immediately
Reposition medially to avoid the carotid artery
Inject anyway at a slower rate
questions.explanation: Blood means reposition medially to avoid the carotid.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal block, aspiration returns air rather than blood. What does that finding imply about needle depth?
options: The needle is in the esophagus
The needle is too deep; withdraw
The needle is in the carotid
The needle is in the correct place
questions.explanation: Air means too deep.

questions.stem: For bilateral glossopharyngeal blockade, what lidocaine volume and concentration should be injected per side?
questions.explanation: Inject 1–2 mL of 2% lidocaine per side.

questions.stem: A patient needs blockade of supraglottic sensation via the superior laryngeal nerve. Which landmark should guide needle placement?
options: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
questions.explanation: The SLN block uses the greater cornu of the hyoid.

questions.stem: A superior laryngeal block fails to anesthetize the supraglottic mucosa. Which branch was most likely missed?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The internal branch provides supraglottic sensation.

questions.stem: After a successful superior laryngeal nerve block, which region should have diminished sensation?
options: Anterior tongue and floor of the mouth
questions.explanation: The SLN block anesthetizes the supraglottic region.

questions.stem: Which injection sequence best matches the lecture technique for superior laryngeal nerve blockade?
options: Inject 1 mL above the membrane, advance 2–3 mm, then inject 2 mL
Inject 5 mL through the cricothyroid membrane
Inject 1 mL into the palatoglossal arch
questions.explanation: Inject 1 mL above the membrane, then advance and inject 2 mL more.

questions.stem: To anesthetize the trachea below the cords, through which membrane is a transtracheal block performed?
options: At the base of the tongue
At the greater cornu of the hyoid
questions.explanation: The transtracheal block goes through the cricothyroid membrane.

questions.stem: During a transtracheal block, what finding confirms that the needle or catheter tip has entered the tracheal lumen?
options: A loss of resistance to saline
questions.explanation: Air aspiration confirms tracheal placement.

questions.stem: Why is local anesthetic injected during inspiration during a transtracheal block?
options: During expiration, to avoid a cough
questions.explanation: Inject during inspiration; the cough spreads anesthetic.

questions.stem: Which lidocaine dose best matches the lecture technique for transtracheal blockade?
questions.explanation: A syringe with 3–5 mL of 2% lidocaine is used.

questions.stem: A patient coughs forcefully after transtracheal injection. Why is an angiocatheter preferred over a rigid needle for this step?
options: It gives faster onset of anesthesia at the cords
It prevents the patient from coughing
A softer catheter reduces trauma during coughing
questions.explanation: A softer angiocatheter reduces mucosal injury.

questions.stem: A transtracheal block most directly anesthetizes which sensory distribution?
options: Recurrent laryngeal distribution below the cords
questions.explanation: It anesthetizes the trachea and cords (RLN region).

questions.stem: A patient still gags during awake intubation after a transtracheal block alone. Which broader strategy provides more complete airway anesthesia?
options: Transtracheal block alone for the whole airway
Topical plus glossopharyngeal, SLN, and transtracheal blocks
Glossopharyngeal block alone for the whole airway
SLN block alone for the whole upper airway
questions.explanation: Combining topical and nerve blocks provides complete anesthesia.

questions.stem: Which historical pairing correctly identifies the origin of the cricoid-pressure maneuver used during RSI?
questions.explanation: Sellick described cricoid pressure in 1961. Macintosh designed the curved blade, and Brain the LMA.

questions.stem: Before loss of consciousness during RSI, what cricoid force does this lecture recommend?
questions.explanation: 10–20 N before LOC, 30–40 N after.

questions.stem: After loss of consciousness during RSI, what cricoid force does this lecture recommend?
questions.explanation: 30–40 N after LOC.

questions.stem: In Sellick's original description, which patient position accompanied application of cricoid pressure?
questions.explanation: Sellick described cricoid pressure with the patient in a 20-degree head-up position.

questions.stem: MRI shows the esophagus lateral to the cricoid cartilage in many patients. Why does that matter when interpreting cricoid pressure?
options: The esophagus is displaced laterally in many patients
The esophagus is completely occluded in nearly all patients
The esophagus does not change position
The trachea collapses in most patients
questions.explanation: MRI shows the esophagus shifts laterally in 50–90%.

questions.stem: Cricoid pressure is increased beyond 40 N while the patient is still responsive. Which adverse effect becomes more likely?
options: Hypertension and tachycardia from sympathetic surge
questions.explanation: Excessive pressure can cause discomfort or retching.

questions.stem: During RSI, forceful cricoid pressure worsens the glottic view and mask ventilation. Which FOUR complications are recognized consequences? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure can obstruct the airway, impair ventilation and the view, and prolong intubation.

questions.stem: When teaching the feel of recommended cricoid force, which bedside comparison is commonly used in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Recommended cricoid pressure feels like firm pressure on the nasal bridge.

questions.stem: Which THREE roles are appropriate uses of a supraglottic airway device? (Select 3)
options: Alternative to ETT for elective surgery
Protection against aspiration in full stomach
questions.explanation: SGDs are for rescue, elective use, and as an intubation conduit.

questions.stem: Which historical timeline for the laryngeal mask airway is correct?
questions.explanation: The LMA was introduced in 1981 and used widely in the US since 1989.

questions.stem: An experienced anesthesia provider inserts an LMA for routine elective surgery. Which first-attempt success range is most consistent with expected performance?
questions.explanation: First-attempt LMA success for experienced providers is about 88–95%.

questions.stem: An LMA is functioning, but cuff pressure measures 75 cmH2O. Which threshold has been exceeded and should prompt correction?
questions.explanation: Avoid overinflation >60 cmH2O, which can open the esophagus.

questions.stem: Standard LMA insertion fails repeatedly because the distal tip folds. Which FOUR alternative insertion techniques can help? (Select 4)
options: Insertion with the cuff fully inflated
questions.explanation: Alternatives include tongue blade help, 180-degree rotation, partial inflation, and guided insertion.

questions.stem: Compared with first-generation SGAs, which FOUR design features characterize second-generation devices? (Select 4)
options: Enhanced cuff design for higher seal pressures
questions.explanation: Second-gen SGAs add gastric channels, reinforced tips, better cuffs, and more rigidity.

questions.stem: A ProSeal is being used where higher airway pressures are expected. Approximately what seal pressure can it support?
questions.explanation: ProSeal supports peak pressures up to 28–30 cmH2O.

questions.stem: A second-generation SGA is needed for a case with moderate positive-pressure ventilation. Which seal pressure best matches the LMA Supreme?
questions.explanation: The Supreme has slightly lower seal pressures (26–28 cmH2O) than ProSeal.

questions.stem: When weighing SGA aspiration risk in a properly selected patient, which incidence best reflects the lecture data?
questions.explanation: Aspiration risk is low, ~1–2 per 10,000.

questions.stem: Which THREE scenarios make an SGA a poor choice as the primary airway? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: SGAs are avoided with subglottic obstruction, active aspiration, and in obstetric patients because they do not protect the airway.

questions.stem: An SGA is malpositioned and its cuff overinflated. Which THREE problems can result? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Malposition or overinflation compromise seal, gastric drainage, and airway patency.

questions.stem: Which description best matches the standard Eschmann bougie used for difficult intubation?
options: 40 cm long with a 60° angled tip
60 cm long with a 40° angled tip
30 cm long with a 90° angled tip
100 cm long with a straight tip
questions.explanation: The bougie is 60 cm with a 40° tip.

questions.stem: A Cormack-Lehane IIb/III view is obtained, but the epiglottis or posterior glottic structures are visible. Which adjunct is most useful?
options: When the glottis is hard to see, like CL IIb or III
When the view is CL grade I with full cords
When the patient is awake and cooperative
For nasal intubation, as a guide through the nose
questions.explanation: Bougies help with poor glottic views.

questions.stem: While advancing a bougie through a limited glottic view, which tactile sign supports tracheal rather than esophageal placement?
questions.explanation: Clicks against tracheal rings suggest tracheal placement.

questions.stem: A bougie is advanced farther than necessary during intubation. Which lip-depth target should generally prevent excessive insertion?
questions.explanation: The 25-cm mark at the lips is ideal.

questions.stem: The ETT repeatedly catches while being railroaded over a correctly placed bougie. What is the best next maneuver?
options: Remove the bougie and try blind
Rotate the ETT 90° to the left
Rotate the ETT 180° to the right
questions.explanation: Rotate 90° counterclockwise to free the bevel.

questions.stem: A legacy airway device confirmed tracheal placement by producing a bright anterior-neck glow. Which device was this?
options: A device using neck transillumination for ETT placement
A videolaryngoscope with a lighted blade tip
A fiberoptic scope used for nasal intubation
A bougie with a light at the tip for blind placement
questions.explanation: It used a glow on the anterior neck to confirm tracheal placement.

questions.stem: Why did lighted stylets such as the Trachlite fall out of routine use?
options: It caused tracheal perforation in most patients
Shift toward fiberoptic and video tools
questions.explanation: It was discontinued in 2009 as fiberoptic and video tools took over.

questions.stem: An airway exchange catheter is left after extubation to preserve reintubation access. Where should its distal tip ideally rest?
questions.explanation: AEC tips are placed just above the carina.

questions.stem: Which airway exchange catheter sizes are generally well tolerated in adults when left temporarily after extubation?
questions.explanation: 11F and 14F are well tolerated.

questions.stem: Why is an airway exchange catheter better tolerated than a bougie when left in place after difficult extubation?
options: It can permit breathing, phonation, and secretion clearance
It is intentionally much stiffer than a bougie
It must be removed immediately after extubation
It cannot serve as a guide for reintubation
questions.explanation: AECs allow spontaneous breathing, speech, and secretion clearance.

questions.stem: Jet ventilation through an airway exchange catheter is planned. Why might neuromuscular relaxation be required?
questions.explanation: Muscle relaxation can prevent glottic closure during jet insufflation.

questions.stem: Before railroading an ETT over an airway exchange catheter, which size relationship must be verified?
options: ETT cuff pressure to the AEC size
ETT curvature to the AEC curvature at the glottis
ETT internal diameter to AEC external diameter
ETT length to AEC length for depth
questions.explanation: Match ETT ID to AEC OD.

questions.stem: Which THREE scenarios are appropriate indications for flexible-scope intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: FIS is indicated for anticipated difficult airways, C-spine immobilization, restricted opening, and failed intubation with ventilation.

questions.stem: Which THREE situations make flexible-scope intubation a poor or unsafe primary rescue technique? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Avoid in epiglottitis, burns, trauma, uncooperative or hypoxic patients, and CICV.

questions.stem: During flexible-scope intubation, the tip is aligned vertically but needs lateral steering. Which movement provides that control?
questions.explanation: The lever controls up/down; wrist rotation controls lateral movement.

questions.stem: A prolonged flexible-scope attempt is limited by secretions and declining oxygen reserve. What is the main advantage of oxygen insufflation through the suction port?
options: Support oxygenation and clear the lens
questions.explanation: O2 insufflation at 2–4 L/min helps oxygenation and clears the lens.

questions.stem: An awake oral flexible-scope intubation is planned in a patient who may bite the scope. Which airway adjuncts are specifically designed to protect and guide it?
questions.explanation: FIS-compatible oral airways include Williams and Ovassapian.

questions.stem: The flexible scope repeatedly fogs on entry despite a clear airway. Which preparation best reduces this problem?
options: Warm saline soak or antifog agent
questions.explanation: Warm saline or antifog agents help.

questions.stem: Which THREE features are true advantages of videolaryngoscopy over direct laryngoscopy? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: VL offers magnified view, team viewing, and easier learning.
