questions.stem: Which TWO limitations should still be anticipated when choosing videolaryngoscopy? (Select 2)
options: View obscured by blood or secretions
Inability to use a stylet with the tube
questions.explanation: VL is costly, and blood or secretions can obscure the camera. Blind tube advancement past the tonsils can injure the pharynx.

questions.stem: A styleted ETT is advanced while attention is fixed on the VL monitor, and resistance is felt near the tonsillar pillar. Which injury is specifically associated with this mechanism?
options: Soft palate or tonsillar pillar perforation
Vocal cord paralysis from nerve stretch
questions.explanation: Indirect ETT/stylet placement can perforate the soft palate or pillars.

questions.stem: A trainee wants to abandon direct-laryngoscopy practice because videolaryngoscopy is available. Which advice best supports safe rescue capability?
options: Keep skills in both DL and VL, since either can be the rescue
VL has fully replaced DL in modern practice
Use DL as the primary device and VL only for rescue
VL should be reserved for airway experts
questions.explanation: Proficiency in both DL and VL is needed, since either may be the rescue technique when the other fails.

questions.stem: A hyperangulated GlideScope gives an excellent view but a straight ETT will not follow the visualized path. What is the main reason?
options: The blade has only a slight 15° curve
The tube must approximate the blade's steep anterior curvature
questions.explanation: The hyperangulated blade has a 60° anterior bend.

questions.stem: A GlideScope image remains clear despite warm humid breath. Which feature helps prevent fogging?
questions.explanation: GlideScope uses a heated lens.

questions.stem: A McGrath blade resists fogging without an active heater. Which design feature accounts for this?
options: Heated lens that warms the camera
questions.explanation: McGrath uses a hydrophilic coating rather than a heater.

questions.stem: You want a video system that can use familiar Macintosh/Miller geometry but also hyperangulated blades and recording. Which device best fits?
questions.explanation: The C-MAC offers standard and hyperangulated blades and recording.

questions.stem: A portable VL is needed for transport and remote locations without an external monitor. Which device best fits that need?
questions.explanation: McGrath has a self-contained rotatable LCD.

questions.stem: A hyperangulated GlideScope view is excellent, but tube delivery is expected to be difficult. How should the ETT be prepared?
options: No stylet and a straight, unshaped tube
questions.explanation: Use a rigid stylet or preshaped ETT.

questions.stem: During GlideScope insertion, the operator keeps looking directly into the mouth and overshoots the epiglottis. What technique would reduce this error?
options: Insert to the right and sweep the tongue
Insert midline and look at the monitor early
Insert laterally and look in the mouth first
questions.explanation: Insert the GlideScope midline and shift to the monitor early to avoid passing structures.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation and intubation have both failed and oxygenation cannot be restored. Which situation now mandates front-of-neck rescue?
options: Routine difficult intubation with good ventilation
Nasal intubation failure with good mask ventilation
questions.explanation: FONA is a rescue for CICO.

questions.stem: Which THREE scenarios are accepted indications for emergency cricothyrotomy? (Select 3)
options: Facial or neck trauma preventing oral/nasal access
questions.explanation: Indications include CICO, trauma preventing access, and immediate obstruction.

questions.stem: Which THREE approaches represent the major cricothyrotomy techniques? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Techniques are needle, percutaneous, and surgical.

questions.stem: Needle cricothyrotomy is chosen for emergency oxygenation. Which catheter characteristic is recommended?
options: 24G IV catheter from the standard IV cart
questions.explanation: Use a large-bore (≥18G) kink-resistant catheter.

questions.stem: Why are standard peripheral IV angiocatheters poor choices for transtracheal jet ventilation?
options: They are too short to reach the trachea
They are too large for the cricothyroid membrane
questions.explanation: Standard angiocaths risk kinking.

questions.stem: A jet injector is connected for transtracheal ventilation. Which driving pressure range is typically used?
questions.explanation: Jet injectors use high-pressure O2 at 50–100 psi.

questions.stem: During transtracheal jet ventilation, what breath frequency best limits air trapping while maintaining oxygenation?
questions.explanation: Deliver low-frequency breaths at 8–10/min.

questions.stem: Which inspiratory-to-expiratory ratio best allows adequate passive exhalation during TTJV?
questions.explanation: I:E ratio is 1:3 to 1:4.

questions.stem: How long should each inspiratory jet generally last during TTJV?
questions.explanation: Inspiratory time is 0.5–1 sec.

questions.stem: Before delivering the next jet breath, chest recoil has not completed. Why should the next breath be delayed?
options: To increase oxygen delivery on the next breath
To prevent air trapping and barotrauma
questions.explanation: Exhalation is passive via the upper airway; incomplete exhalation causes air trapping.

questions.stem: During TTJV, exhalation becomes severely impaired by upper-airway obstruction. Which complication is the most immediate life threat?
questions.explanation: Barotrauma is the most serious concern.

questions.stem: Which FOUR complications are recognized risks of TTJV, especially when gas egress is limited? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: TTJV risks barotrauma, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and hypercarbia.

questions.stem: Because the transtracheal catheter is used mainly for insufflation, how does exhalation normally occur during TTJV?
questions.explanation: Exhalation is passive via the upper airway.

questions.stem: Which THREE pieces of equipment are central to retrograde intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Equipment includes a catheter, wire/suture, Magill forceps, and ETT.

questions.stem: During retrograde intubation, in which direction should the cricothyroid needle be angled to direct the guide cephalad?
questions.explanation: The needle is angled cephalad.

questions.stem: Visual intubation has failed, but mask ventilation remains effective. In which situation could retrograde intubation still be considered?
options: Visual intubation fails but ventilation is adequate
CICO with no ventilation possible at all
Routine elective intubation in a healthy patient
questions.explanation: It is useful when visual methods fail but ventilation is possible.

questions.stem: A surgical tracheotomy is planned rather than an emergency cricothyrotomy. At which tracheal-ring level is the opening typically created?
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy is typically at rings 4–6.

questions.stem: A CICO emergency requires immediate airway access. Why is surgical tracheotomy generally not the first emergency choice?
options: It is less invasive than a cricothyrotomy
It is performed in pediatric patients
It takes up to 30 minutes and needs a surgical team
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy takes time and requires a controlled environment.

questions.stem: Which TWO complications are specifically associated with tracheotomy? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Tracheotomy complications include RLN injury and innominate artery injury, along with esophageal trauma, infection, bleeding, and tracheal stenosis.

questions.stem: In a true emergency front-of-neck airway, which structure is the primary target?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane is the FONA target.

questions.stem: In an obese patient with poorly palpable neck landmarks, how can ultrasound most directly improve FONA preparation?
options: Locating the cricothyroid membrane in difficult anatomy
Guiding jet ventilation pressures and the respiratory rate
questions.explanation: Ultrasound helps locate the membrane and may reduce misplacement.

questions.stem: Which THREE outcomes are central goals of extubation planning rather than simply removing the tube early? (Select 3)
options: Extubate as early as possible in all cases
questions.explanation: Planning aims to reduce disturbances, complications, stay, and costs.

questions.stem: A long neck dissection had an easy intubation, but significant edema is expected. Which principle should guide extubation?
options: Extubation is lower risk than intubation in most patients
Extubation carries significant risk and needs a plan
Extubation is safer than intubation in every case
questions.explanation: Extubation is not benign. Airway edema, surgery, and residual drugs can make it more dangerous than intubation.

questions.stem: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring shows a TOF ratio of 0.82 before extubation. How should this be interpreted?
options: Yes; a ratio above 0.3 is adequate here
No; the TOF ratio should exceed 0.9
Yes; a ratio above 0.5 is adequate
Yes; a ratio above 0.7 is adequate
questions.explanation: Adequate reversal requires a TOF ratio greater than 0.9.

questions.stem: Which FIVE findings support adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation? (Select 5)
options: Head lift for more than 5 seconds
Sustained tetanus at 100 Hz for 5 seconds
questions.explanation: Criteria include TOFR >0.9, 100 Hz tetanus 5 s, DBS without fade, 5-s head lift, and strong grip.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient has a vital capacity of 900 mL before extubation. How does this compare with the target threshold?
options: No; it should exceed 30 mL/kg, or 2,100 mL
No; it should exceed 15 mL/kg, or 1,050 mL
questions.explanation: Vital capacity should exceed 15 mL/kg; 900 mL is about 13 mL/kg.

questions.stem: A patient generates a negative inspiratory force of −14 cmH2O. What does this imply about extubation readiness?
options: Inadequate; NIF should be more negative than −60 cmH2O
Adequate; NIF should be more positive than +20 cmH2O
Inadequate; NIF should be more negative than −20 cmH2O
Adequate; it is more negative than −5 cmH2O
questions.explanation: NIF should be more negative than −20 cmH2O before extubation.

questions.stem: An 80-kg patient has spontaneous tidal volumes of 250 mL. Does this satisfy the usual extubation target?
options: No; tidal volume should be at least 15 mL/kg
No; tidal volume should be at least 4–5 mL/kg (320–400 mL)
No; tidal volume should be at least 10–12 mL/kg
questions.explanation: Spontaneous tidal volume should be at least 4–5 mL/kg; 250 mL is about 3 mL/kg.

questions.stem: On FiO2 0.40, SpO2 is 93% and PaO2 is 72 mmHg. Do these oxygenation values meet the lecture's extubation criteria?
options: Yes; criteria are SpO2 above 90% and PaO2 above 60 on FiO2 under 50%
No; SpO2 must exceed 99% and PaO2 200
No; PaO2 must exceed 100 mmHg on any FiO2 before extubation
questions.explanation: Oxygenation criteria for extubation are SpO2 above 90% and PaO2 above 60 mmHg with FiO2 below 50%.

questions.stem: Which FOUR global conditions should be present before extubation? (Select 4)
options: Return of laryngeal and cough reflexes
questions.explanation: Global criteria include hemodynamic stability, normothermia, patent airway with reflexes, strength, and metabolic stability.

questions.stem: A patient meets standard criteria but develops respiratory failure minutes after extubation. What does this illustrate about extubation?
options: It tests neuromuscular function and nothing else
It carries no risk once criteria are met
questions.explanation: Extubation itself tests whether spontaneous ventilation and cardiopulmonary function can be sustained.

questions.stem: Which Guedel stage should be avoided for extubation because airway reflexes are hyperactive and laryngospasm risk is high?
questions.explanation: Avoid extubation in stage II due to laryngospasm risk.

questions.stem: For a routine patient, which timing choices are generally safest for extubation?
options: Deeply anesthetized (stage III) or fully awake
During stage II excitement, as reflexes return
As soon as spontaneous breathing starts
questions.explanation: Extubate deep in stage III or fully awake.

questions.stem: A patient is at high risk for reintubation difficulty. When should extubation occur?
options: Deep in stage III to avoid any coughing on the tube
When reflexes return and ventilation is adequate
questions.explanation: High-risk patients should be extubated awake with reflexes and adequate ventilation.

questions.stem: Which FOUR drug classes can blunt the cardiovascular response to awake extubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, CCBs, and vasodilators blunt the response.

questions.stem: Which THREE strategies can reduce coughing and straining during extubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics and cautious opioids reduce coughing.

questions.stem: Why should the extubation/recovery phase receive the same attention as induction in airway planning?
questions.explanation: Up to 1/3 of airway emergencies occur at extubation/recovery.

questions.stem: Which FOUR techniques are reasonable for extubating a high-risk airway while preserving rescue options? (Select 4)
options: Use of an airway exchange catheter
questions.explanation: Options include FIS, SGA exchange, AEC, or delayed extubation.

questions.stem: Before extubating a known difficult airway, what team action is most important?
options: Avoid telling the team to reduce anxiety
Discuss contingency plans with the team
questions.explanation: Always discuss contingency plans with the OR team before extubation.

questions.stem: Which FOUR patient factors increase the risk of difficult extubation or reintubation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Patient risk factors include difficult reintubation evaluation, illnesses, edema, cervical limitation, and tracheomalacia.

questions.stem: Which FIVE surgical factors increase the likelihood of a difficult extubation? (Select 5)
options: Airway or head and neck surgery
questions.explanation: Surgical risk factors include airway/head and neck surgery, neurosurgery, prolonged duration, and prone/Trendelenburg.

questions.stem: Which FOUR anesthetic factors should increase concern about extubation failure? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Anesthetic factors include difficult intubation, excessive fluids, lack of cuff leak, and laryngotracheal edema.

questions.stem: A patient has no cuff leak after prolonged airway surgery. What is the most concerning interpretation?
questions.explanation: Lack of cuff leak suggests laryngotracheal edema.

questions.stem: Which THREE complications are consistent with residual neuromuscular blockade after extubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Residual block causes obstruction, hypoxemia, aspiration risk, blunted hypoxic response, and weakness.

questions.stem: Rocuronium effect is rapidly reversed with sugammadex. What mechanism explains this reversal?
options: Cyclodextrin encapsulation that inactivates the drug
questions.explanation: Sugammadex traps and inactivates rocuronium/vecuronium.

questions.stem: Immediately after extubation, the patient makes forceful inspiratory efforts but no air moves and the cords are tightly closed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is involuntary forceful laryngeal contraction.

questions.stem: When laryngospasm occurs, approximately how often can oxygen desaturation develop?
questions.explanation: Desaturation occurs in up to 60%.

questions.stem: Which sensory-motor reflex pathway most directly mediates laryngospasm?
options: SLN afferent to RLN motor response
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is triggered by vagal stimulation along the SLN→RLN pathway.

questions.stem: Complete airway closure occurs from extrinsic laryngeal muscle contraction. Which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Ball-valve closure (extrinsic muscles) is complete; glottic shutter (intrinsic) is partial.

questions.stem: Partial glottic closure occurs from intrinsic laryngeal muscle contraction. Which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Glottic shutter is intrinsic and partial.

questions.stem: Which THREE conditions commonly trigger laryngospasm around extubation? (Select 3)
options: Blood or secretions on the cords
questions.explanation: Causes include manipulation, noxious stimuli, and light anesthesia.

questions.stem: Persistent laryngospasm continues despite CPAP. Jaw thrust plus firm pressure at the laryngospasm notch is applied. Which maneuver is being used?
questions.explanation: Larson maneuver is jaw thrust plus pressure at the laryngospasm notch.

questions.stem: Laryngospasm persists despite airway-opening maneuvers and positive pressure, and SpO2 continues to fall. Which medication should be given next?
questions.explanation: Give succinylcholine immediately if desaturation persists.

questions.stem: After a severe laryngospasm episode with strong inspiratory efforts against a closed glottis, which pulmonary complication is a major concern?
questions.explanation: Address hypoxia and prevent NPPE.

questions.stem: A child develops inspiratory stridor after extubation due to subglottic edema. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Croup is subglottic inflammation and edema.

questions.stem: Which TWO findings most strongly support postextubation croup rather than bronchospasm? (Select 2)
options: Expiratory wheeze with a prolonged I:E ratio
questions.explanation: Postextubation croup causes inspiratory stridor and a barking cough from subglottic edema.

questions.stem: A child is extubated uneventfully but develops barky cough and stridor shortly afterward. When does postextubation croup most commonly appear?
questions.explanation: Croup typically occurs within 3 hours.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors increase the risk of postextubation croup? (Select 4)
options: Airway edema from trauma or positioning
questions.explanation: Causes include edema, multiple attempts, oversized ETT, and excess movement.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops barky cough and stridor in PACU. Which nebulized racemic epinephrine dose matches the lecture?
options: 2 mL of 0.5% epinephrine in 5 mL NS, nebulized
0.5 mL of 2.25% in 2.5 mL NS, nebulized
questions.explanation: Postextubation croup is treated with nebulized racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% in 2.5 mL NS.

questions.stem: A 15-kg child has postextubation croup. Which dexamethasone dose range is appropriate?
options: 15–30 mg (1–2 mg/kg), given IV over 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone 0.1–0.5 mg/kg reduces airway edema; for 15 kg that is 1.5–7.5 mg.

questions.stem: Heliox is chosen as an adjunct for croup. What physical property makes it useful?
options: Its low density reduces airflow resistance
It raises inspired oxygen content above 100%
questions.explanation: Helium lowers gas density and resistance.

questions.stem: Why does a similar degree of subglottic edema create more severe obstruction in children than adults?
questions.explanation: Small airways increase resistance with edema.

questions.stem: Which airway-related injury accounts for the greatest number of anesthesia malpractice claims?
questions.explanation: Dental injury is the most common claim.

questions.stem: During laryngoscopy, which teeth are most vulnerable to injury from improper blade leverage?
options: Mandibular molars on the right side
questions.explanation: Maxillary central incisors are most often affected.

questions.stem: Weeks after a difficult intubation, a patient remains hoarse with a weak voice. Which THREE laryngeal injuries could explain this? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Laryngeal trauma from intubation includes cord paralysis, granulomas, and arytenoid dislocation.

questions.stem: After traumatic intubation, which combination of findings should raise concern for esophageal perforation?
options: Normal exam without symptoms in most cases
questions.explanation: Esophageal injury signs include neck edema, subcutaneous emphysema, and pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Why does suspected esophageal perforation require urgent treatment even after the airway has been secured?
options: The main consequence is transient dysphagia
questions.explanation: Mediastinitis has ~50% mortality.

questions.stem: Which FIVE factors increase the risk of tracheal injury during or after intubation? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Tracheal injury risk rises with overinflated cuffs, multiple attempts, large ETTs, stylets, steroids, and COPD.

questions.stem: Clinically significant pulmonary aspiration is uncommon. Which incidence best matches the lecture data?
questions.explanation: Clinically significant aspiration is ~1 in 35,000.

questions.stem: After gastric aspiration, what is the expected sequence of lung injury?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is chemical injury; phase 2 is inflammation.

questions.stem: During mask ventilation of a full-stomach patient, which pressure range should generally not be exceeded to limit gastric insufflation and aspiration risk?
questions.explanation: Limit mask pressures to <15–20 cmH2O.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis is scheduled for GA. Which FOUR medications can reduce aspiration risk or severity? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Aspiration prophylaxis includes nonparticulate antacids, H2 blockers, PPIs, and prokinetics.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease and suspected gastric stasis needs aspiration prophylaxis. Which commonly used prokinetic should be avoided?
options: Asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in bowel obstruction and Parkinson's.

questions.stem: After intubation, chest rise and bilateral breath sounds are present but are not definitive. Which finding most reliably confirms tracheal placement?
questions.explanation: Capnography is most reliable.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings may falsely reassure the provider about ETT placement and therefore should not be used alone? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Breath sounds, chest movement, fog, and epigastric auscultation are unreliable.

questions.stem: When capnography is equivocal and direct confirmation is needed, which additional method is highly sensitive for verifying tracheal placement?
options: Palpating the cuff in the neck
questions.explanation: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy is sensitive but not always practical.

questions.stem: Which FIVE complications can result from unrecognized or traumatic esophageal intubation? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Complications include perforation, abscess, emphysema, pneumothorax, and mediastinitis.

questions.stem: Which airway error is a major contributor to severe respiratory closed claims because it can be missed despite misleading physical signs?
questions.explanation: Unrecognized esophageal intubation is a significant contributor to respiratory closed claims.

questions.stem: Which THREE complications should remain on the immediate differential after tracheal intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Intubation complications include airway trauma, aspiration, esophageal and endobronchial intubation, and ETT problems.

questions.stem: Which THREE practices reduce airway-management complications during repeated or difficult intubation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Prevention includes careful technique, limited attempts, and cuff monitoring.

questions.stem: A bearded patient with BMI 38, OSA, Mallampati IV, TMD 5 cm, and neck circumference 46 cm presents for GA. Which THREE airway tasks are predicted to be difficult? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Beard, obesity, and OSA predict difficult BMV; Mallampati IV and short TMD predict difficult laryngoscopy; obesity and thick neck complicate cric.

questions.stem: In that high-risk patient, which preinduction strategy best preserves options if conventional intubation fails?
options: Standard induction with a Mac 3 blade
Deep sedation without an airway backup plan
Plan a standard RSI with a Mac blade
Plan awake intubation or have VL, SGA, and FONA ready
questions.explanation: Multiple predictors call for a strategy that preserves spontaneous ventilation or a full backup setup.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient will receive topical lidocaine. Using 4.5 mg/kg as the working maximum, what is the approximate total dose limit?
You draw up 5 mL of 4% lidocaine for topicalization. How many milligrams does this contain?
A nebulizer contains 8 mL of 4% lidocaine. What total lidocaine dose is being delivered?
questions.explanation: 8 mL × 40 mg/mL = 320 mg.

questions.stem: A patient receives 8 mL of 4% lidocaine plus 2 mL of 2% lidocaine for each bilateral SLN block. What is the total dose?
A patient with an unstable cervical spine requires intubation while minimizing neck movement and preserving neurologic assessment. Which technique is best?
options: Blind nasal intubation under deep sedation
Awake flexible scope intubation with topical anesthesia
Direct laryngoscopy with full neck extension
questions.explanation: Unstable C-spine is an indication for awake intubation that preserves spontaneous ventilation and allows a neuro check.

questions.stem: A patient with a large laryngeal tumor and stridor is at risk of losing the airway after induction. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Awake intubation or surgical airway preparation
Rapid sequence induction with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: Airway tumors are indications for awake intubation and FONA readiness.

questions.stem: After induction, bag-mask ventilation remains impossible despite repositioning, OPA, and a two-hand seal while SpO2 falls. What should be done next?
options: Attempt intubation with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: Escalate to SGA when BMV fails.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation and SGA rescue have failed, intubation is unsuccessful, and SpO2 is 70%. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: CICO requires emergency front-of-neck access.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy yields a Cormack-Lehane III view. Which next maneuver best improves the chance of successful intubation without repeated blind attempts?
options: Remove the blade and wake the patient immediately
Switch to a smaller blade without changes
Use a bougie or BURP, or switch to VL
questions.explanation: Poor views benefit from bougie, BURP, or VL.

questions.stem: A Cormack-Lehane IIb view shows only the posterior glottis. Which adjunct is most likely to facilitate tracheal tube placement?
questions.explanation: Bougies are used for IIb/III views.

questions.stem: An ETT catches at the arytenoids while being advanced over a correctly placed bougie. What should be done?
options: Remove the bougie and push harder
Advance the bougie into the bronchus
questions.explanation: Rotate the ETT to free the bevel.

questions.stem: Hyperangulated VL provides an excellent glottic view, but the ETT will not follow the path to the cords. What is the most likely problem?
options: The glottis is not visible on the screen
The patient is in laryngospasm at the cords
The ETT is not shaped to follow the blade's angle
questions.explanation: Hyperangulated VL needs a rigid stylet or preshaped tube.

questions.stem: After VL intubation, a tonsillar pillar is torn. Which technique error most likely caused the injury?
options: Blind ETT advancement while looking at the screen
Excessive cuff pressure against the tonsillar pillar
questions.explanation: VL risks pharyngeal injury from indirect advancement.

questions.stem: A patient has only 2 cm of mouth opening. Which intubation technique is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Restricted mouth opening favors flexible scope; LMA and DL are limited.

questions.stem: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has fixed neck flexion and minimal atlantooccipital extension. Which airway approach is most appropriate?
options: Flexible scope or VL rather than DL
DL with maximal extension of the neck
questions.explanation: Limited AO mobility makes DL difficult; FIS or VL are alternatives.

questions.stem: A term parturient requires emergency general anesthesia. Which airway complication is disproportionately more common in this population?
questions.explanation: CICV incidence is about 1:300 in obstetrics.

questions.stem: During nitrous oxide anesthesia, cuff pressure rises to 45 cmH2O. What should be done?
options: Leave it, since N2O effects are temporary
Deflate the cuff and ventilate around it
Reduce the cuff pressure below 25 cmH2O
Increase the pressure to prevent aspiration
questions.explanation: Keep cuff pressure <25 cmH2O; N2O increases it.

questions.stem: After a short case with an 8.5-mm ETT, the patient reports sore throat and hoarseness. What is the most likely contributing factor?
questions.explanation: Larger ETTs risk trauma, nerve injury, and sore throat.

questions.stem: Which THREE steps are appropriate preparation for nasotracheal intubation? (Select 3)
options: Grab the cuff with Magill forceps
questions.explanation: Prep includes nostril selection, vasoconstrictor, lubrication, bevel away from midline, and floor-of-nose passage.

questions.stem: During nasal intubation, the tube reaches 15 cm and is now in the oropharynx. What should happen next?
options: Push harder through the resistance at 15 cm
Pull back and try the other nostril right away
Perform DL and guide the ETT with Magill forceps
questions.explanation: At 14–16 cm the tube is in the oropharynx; use DL and Magill forceps to guide it.

questions.stem: Heavy epistaxis occurs during nasal intubation. Which preventive step was most likely omitted?
options: Using a larger tube to tamponade bleeding
Advancing along the roof of the nose toward the turbinates
Vasoconstrictor and gentle insertion along the nasal floor
Using a larger ETT to tamponade the mucosa
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors and proper technique reduce bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient with basilar skull fracture requires airway control. Why should nasotracheal intubation be avoided?
options: Risk of intracranial passage through a skull-base defect
The nasal route always causes aspiration
questions.explanation: Basilar skull fracture is a contraindication to nasotracheal intubation because a tube may pass intracranially through a disrupted skull base.

questions.stem: A nasal ETT is advanced with its bevel facing the septum. Which complication is this technique more likely to cause?
options: Turbinate or septal mucosal trauma and epistaxis
questions.explanation: The nasal ETT bevel should face away from the septum to reduce mucosal and turbinate trauma and epistaxis.

questions.stem: A patient with anticipated difficult intubation is undergoing awake nasal fiberoptic intubation. Which premedication helps improve visualization by drying secretions?
questions.explanation: An antisialagogue such as glycopyrrolate dries secretions and improves visualization during awake flexible-scope intubation.

questions.stem: During awake intubation, excessive sedation causes airway obstruction and hypoventilation. Which principle was violated?
options: Use a long-acting opioid for comfort
Avoid deep sedation that can collapse the airway
Give deep sedation for comfort during scoping
questions.explanation: Deep sedation during awake intubation risks airway collapse.

questions.stem: During awake airway topicalization, total lidocaine from all routes approaches the calculated maximum. What is the safest action?
options: Stop adding lidocaine and use non-local-anesthetic adjuncts as needed
Continue because topical lidocaine has no systemic maximum
Add benzocaine without considering cumulative toxicity
Double the remaining dose because airway absorption is negligible
questions.explanation: All lidocaine routes contribute to the cumulative dose; approaching the maximum should prompt stopping further lidocaine and avoiding local-anesthetic systemic toxicity.

questions.stem: A patient receives topical benzocaine and develops cyanosis with unexpectedly preserved PaO2. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia, producing cyanosis despite an adequate PaO2.

questions.stem: A glossopharyngeal block is planned to suppress gagging during awake intubation. Which sensory territory is the primary target?
options: Posterior one-third of the tongue and oropharynx
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal blockade anesthetizes the posterior tongue and oropharynx and helps suppress gagging.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal block, blood is aspirated before injection. What should be done next?
options: Do not inject; reposition away from the vessel and re-aspirate
Inject slowly because blood confirms the target
Advance deeper until air is aspirated
Convert the injection to an intravascular test dose
questions.explanation: Blood aspiration indicates vascular placement; injection should be withheld and the needle repositioned before re-aspiration.

questions.stem: After bilateral superior laryngeal blocks, which airway region should have reduced sensation?
options: Supraglottic larynx above the vocal cords
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies sensation to the supraglottic larynx.

questions.stem: During transtracheal injection, the patient coughs vigorously. Why is this response desirable?
options: Coughing disperses local anesthetic over the vocal cords and tracheal mucosa
It proves the patient is deeply anesthetized
questions.explanation: Transtracheal lidocaine is injected during inspiration; the resulting cough helps spread local anesthetic over the cords and trachea.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing awake intubation still has intact sensation below the vocal cords despite good oropharyngeal and supraglottic anesthesia. Which block is missing?
questions.explanation: A transtracheal block anesthetizes the recurrent-laryngeal sensory distribution at and below the vocal cords.

questions.stem: A patient with difficult laryngoscopy has successful mask ventilation. Which principle should guide repeated attempts?
options: Reoxygenate between attempts and change technique rather than repeating ineffective laryngoscopy
Continue attempts without interruption while mask ventilation remains possible
Avoid alternative devices until direct laryngoscopy has failed at least five times
Paralyze more deeply before every repeated attempt regardless of cause
questions.explanation: When oxygenation is possible, restore oxygenation between attempts and use a changed or improved strategy rather than accumulating trauma with repeated identical attempts.

questions.stem: A difficult-airway attempt has already failed twice with worsening edema and trauma. What is the best next strategy?
options: Change approach and use the best available alternative technique
Repeat the identical attempt because prior failure predicts eventual success
Continue until edema prevents further instrumentation
Remove all rescue devices to simplify the setup
questions.explanation: Repeated failed attempts increase trauma and edema; after failures, change technique and escalate to the best alternative approach.

questions.stem: After a difficult intubation is finally successful, what should be documented and communicated for future anesthetics?
options: The difficulty encountered, devices/techniques used, successful rescue, and recommendations for future airway management
questions.explanation: A difficult airway should be clearly documented and communicated, including what was difficult, what worked, and recommendations for future anesthetics.

questions.stem: Prior neck radiation and a large goiter are present. Which rescue technique should be assumed technically difficult even before induction?
questions.explanation: Radiation and tumor (SHORT) predict difficult cric.

questions.stem: In morbid obesity, the cricothyroid membrane cannot be palpated reliably. Which adjunct best identifies the target before an emergency occurs?
questions.explanation: POCUS helps locate the membrane in obese patients.

questions.stem: During TTJV, the chest fails to recoil between breaths. What complication is developing?
options: Hypocarbia from overventilation through the catheter
questions.explanation: Incomplete exhalation causes air trapping and barotrauma.

questions.stem: Which TWO TTJV settings best promote adequate exhalation and reduce air trapping? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: TTJV uses a low rate of 8–10/min and an I:E of 1:3 to 1:4 so trapped gas can escape through the upper airway.

questions.stem: During TTJV, the neck becomes swollen with palpable crepitus. Which complication has occurred?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema is a TTJV complication.

questions.stem: During retrograde intubation, the guidewire has been retrieved from the mouth. What should be done at the neck before railroading the ETT?
options: Cut the wire flush with skin
Clamp the wire to prevent migration
Remove the wire immediately after retrieval
questions.explanation: Clamp the wire at the neck, then railroad the ETT.

questions.stem: During retrograde intubation, the ETT is advanced over the wire until resistance is encountered. What is the next step?
options: Remove the wire at the neck, then advance the ETT
Withdraw the ETT and wire together
Inflate the cuff before removing the wire
Advance the wire farther into the trachea
questions.explanation: When resistance is met during ETT advancement, remove the retrograde wire at the neck and then advance the ETT farther into the trachea.

questions.stem: A trauma patient will require prolonged mechanical ventilation. Which definitive airway is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Long-term ventilation is a tracheotomy indication.

questions.stem: Which major vascular injury is a recognized complication of tracheotomy?
questions.explanation: Major vascular injury includes the innominate artery.

questions.stem: A healthy, fasted patient is having a short knee arthroscopy. Which airway option is most appropriate if no additional risk factors are present?
options: LMA as an alternative to an ETT
questions.explanation: SGAs are an alternative to ETTs for elective surgery.

questions.stem: An SGA is chosen for laparoscopic surgery where higher seal pressure and gastric drainage are desirable. Which design feature is preferred?
questions.explanation: ProSeal is used in laparoscopic cases with higher seal and gastric drainage.

questions.stem: A term parturient requires emergency general anesthesia. Why is an SGA a poor primary-airway choice in this setting?
options: SGAs are avoided in obstetric patients due to aspiration risk
SGAs cause more airway trauma in pregnancy
SGAs cause hypertension in pregnant patients
SGAs require neuromuscular blockade in pregnancy
questions.explanation: The lecture advises avoiding SGAs in obstetric patients.

questions.stem: A patient has fixed subglottic stenosis. Why may an SGA fail to provide effective ventilation?
options: SGAs cause laryngospasm when stenosis is present
SGAs are too small to seal adult subglottic airways
SGAs require awake placement in all stenosis cases
questions.explanation: SGAs are ineffective with airway pathology below the glottis.

questions.stem: An LMA cuff pressure is 80 cmH2O. Which complication becomes more likely at this level?
options: Lower airway resistance from a wider seal
Opening the upper esophageal sphincter and gastric insufflation
An improved seal with a lower aspiration risk overall
questions.explanation: Overinflation >60 cmH2O can open the esophagus.

questions.stem: An LMA is in place but ventilation is poor with high peak pressure and no obvious circuit problem. Which device problem is most likely?
options: Cuff underinflation, with a normal position
Malposition folding the epiglottis over the glottis
Excellent seal with no leak at peak pressure
Low airway resistance from a wide lumen
questions.explanation: Malposition can obstruct the airway by displacing the epiglottis.

questions.stem: During failed intubation, an SGA is inserted as rescue and oxygenation improves. What is its main advantage in this setting?
options: Fast, easy insertion with high rescue success
It protects against aspiration during rescue
It allows controlled ventilation at high pressures
questions.explanation: SGAs are fast, easy rescue tools with high success.

questions.stem: The team wants an SGA that can also serve as a conduit for tracheal intubation. Which device type best supports that plan?
options: Classic LMA without an intubation conduit
Intubating SGA such as Fastrach or AuraGain
questions.explanation: Some SGAs are designed as intubation conduits.

questions.stem: An LMA leaks at 12 cmH2O despite repositioning. How should this finding change the airway plan?
options: Normal leak pressure for all SGA designs
The patient is ready for extubation and PACU
Difficult SGA ventilation; consider alternative airway
Adequate seal for all ventilation needs
questions.explanation: Leaks <15 cmH2O suggest difficulty.

questions.stem: A difficult-intubation patient has airway edema but otherwise meets extubation criteria. Which strategy best preserves immediate reintubation access?
options: Extubate over an airway exchange catheter
Extubate deep without a backup device
questions.explanation: AECs allow reversible extubation and guided reintubation.

questions.stem: After extubation over an AEC, progressive stridor develops and oxygenation worsens. What is the best use of the catheter now?
options: Reintubate over the AEC with laryngoscope assistance
Remove the AEC and give racemic epinephrine
Advance the AEC into the bronchus
questions.explanation: The AEC guides reintubation.

questions.stem: During reintubation over an AEC, the ETT hangs up at the glottis. What is the best next maneuver?
options: Push harder through the resistance at the glottis
Remove the AEC and try blind
Slightly retract and rotate the ETT 90° counterclockwise
questions.explanation: Retract slightly and rotate 90° counterclockwise.

questions.stem: After head-and-neck surgery, significant airway edema persists despite otherwise adequate recovery. Which extubation decision is most appropriate?
options: Extubate in the OR with a steroid dose
Extubate without a cuff leak test
Extubate deep to avoid coughing on the tube
questions.explanation: Delayed extubation is an option for high-risk patients.

questions.stem: After prolonged prone spine surgery and large-volume resuscitation, there is no cuff leak. What does this suggest?
options: Laryngotracheal edema and high extubation risk
Safe extubation conditions after prone surgery
questions.explanation: Lack of cuff leak suggests edema.

questions.stem: At emergence, TOFR is 0.70, vital capacity is 10 mL/kg, and grip is weak. Should extubation proceed?
options: No; NM strength and VC do not meet criteria
Yes; TOFR above 0.5 is sufficient for extubation
Yes; VC over 5 mL/kg is sufficient
Yes; hand grip is not required
questions.explanation: Criteria require TOFR >0.9 and VC >15 mL/kg.

questions.stem: TOFR is 0.95, vital capacity 18 mL/kg, NIF −30 cmH2O, and SpO2 96% on FiO2 0.40. How should these respiratory criteria be interpreted?
options: No, NIF must be more negative than −60 cmH2O
questions.explanation: These values meet the lecture criteria.

questions.stem: A patient can lift the head for only 2 seconds and has weak hand grip. What does this indicate?
options: Adequate strength for immediate extubation now
questions.explanation: Criteria require head lift >5 seconds and strong grip.

questions.stem: A patient is coughing and moving during Guedel stage II emergence. What is the best extubation strategy?
options: Avoid extubation until deeper or fully awake
Extubate now, since coughing shows reflexes are intact
questions.explanation: Avoid extubating during stage II.

questions.stem: Complete laryngospasm persists with SpO2 80% despite jaw thrust, Larson maneuver, and positive pressure. What should be given next?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is given if desaturation persists.

questions.stem: After severe laryngospasm resolves, pink frothy sputum appears. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: NPPE follows forceful inspiration against a closed glottis.

questions.stem: Which extubation strategy best reduces laryngospasm risk by avoiding airway stimulation during light anesthesia?
options: Suction while the patient is light
Stimulate the airway to trigger waking
Extubate deep in stage III or fully awake
questions.explanation: Avoid airway irritation during light anesthesia.

questions.stem: A child develops stridor 2 hours after multiple traumatic intubation attempts. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Laryngospasm from secretions on the vocal cords
questions.explanation: Croup occurs within 3 hours, especially after multiple attempts.

questions.stem: A child has postextubation croup with stridor but is still moving air adequately. Which initial therapy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate reintubation with a larger tube
questions.explanation: Treatment includes humidified O2, racemic epinephrine, dexamethasone, and heliox.

questions.stem: A 20-kg child with croup needs dexamethasone. Which dose range is appropriate?
Residual neuromuscular blockade causes upper-airway obstruction after extubation. What is the best immediate management?
options: Give flumazenil to reverse residual weakness
Remove oxygen to stimulate the respiratory drive
Support ventilation and reverse with sugammadex if appropriate
Give additional rocuronium to relax the airway
questions.explanation: Residual NMB requires reversal and support.

questions.stem: A maxillary central incisor is chipped during laryngoscopy. Which statement best reflects the malpractice significance of this injury?
options: Dental injury involves molars more than incisors
Dental injury is the most common anesthesia malpractice claim
Dental injury is rare and seldom documented
Dental injury occurs mainly with videolaryngoscopy
questions.explanation: Dental injury is the most common anesthesia claim, most often involving the maxillary incisors.

questions.stem: Persistent hoarseness follows prolonged intubation with a large ETT. Which laryngeal complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: Prolonged intubation and large ETTs can cause granulomas.

questions.stem: After difficult intubation, neck swelling, subcutaneous emphysema, and fever develop. Which complication is most concerning?
options: Laryngospasm from secretions after extubation in PACU
questions.explanation: Esophageal injury can lead to mediastinitis.

questions.stem: After intubation, bilateral breath sounds are heard but no sustained ETCO2 is detected. What should be assumed until proven otherwise?
options: Correct tracheal placement confirmed by sounds
questions.explanation: Breath sounds are unreliable; capnography is most reliable.

questions.stem: The ETT fogs with each breath but ETCO2 remains absent. What should be done?
questions.explanation: Condensation is unreliable; absent ETCO2 suggests esophageal placement.

questions.stem: A full-stomach patient with GERD requires gentle mask ventilation. Which pressure target best limits gastric insufflation?
options: As high as needed to see chest rise
questions.explanation: Limit mask pressures to reduce aspiration.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease needs aspiration prophylaxis. Which medication should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in Parkinson's.

questions.stem: After gastric aspiration during induction, what characterizes phase 1 of aspiration pneumonitis?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is direct chemical injury; phase 2 is inflammation.

questions.stem: Why should airway management in the ICU be approached with a particularly low threshold for rescue planning compared with the OR?
questions.explanation: Adverse airway events are 30–60× more likely in ED/ICU.

questions.stem: A patient with epiglottitis requires airway control. Which technique is specifically discouraged in this lecture?
options: Controlled inhalation induction with surgical backup
questions.explanation: FIS should be avoided in epiglottitis.

questions.stem: A patient with airway burns requires urgent intubation. Which airway tool is specifically not recommended by this lecture?
questions.explanation: FIS is avoided in airway burns per the lecture.

questions.stem: Severe airway bleeding is present. What is the main limitation of videolaryngoscopy in this setting?
options: Blood can obscure the camera view
VL cannot be used with an LMA in place
questions.explanation: Blood and secretions can obscure the VL view.

questions.stem: A CICO emergency is underway. Why is flexible-scope intubation a poor rescue choice now?
options: It is slow and not suited for emergent CICO
It is the fastest emergency method available
questions.explanation: FIS is not ideal for emergent CICO.

questions.stem: Intubation has failed, but an SGA provides effective ventilation. Which next step can use that stable oxygenation to secure the trachea?
options: Intubate through the SGA with a flexible scope
questions.explanation: FIS through an SGA is an option when ventilation is possible.

questions.stem: A cooperative patient has an anticipated difficult airway with high risk if spontaneous ventilation is lost. Which approach best preserves safety?
options: Rapid sequence induction with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: Awake intubation preserves spontaneous ventilation.

questions.stem: During awake fiberoptic intubation, the patient becomes combative and SpO2 falls to 82%. What does this illustrate about patient selection for the technique?
options: It requires deep sedation to succeed
Flexible scopes prevent hypoxia during scoping
Flexible scopes work best in uncooperative, hypoxic patients
questions.explanation: Flexible scope intubation is avoided in uncooperative or severely hypoxic patients because it takes time and cooperation.

questions.stem: Mallampati II, thyromental distance 7 cm, mouth opening 4 cm, and normal neck mobility are all present. What is the best overall interpretation?
questions.explanation: Normal findings predict low difficulty, though no test is perfect.

questions.stem: A patient has a thyromental distance of 10 cm. Which laryngeal position should this make you anticipate?
options: Caudally placed larynx with deep visual field
Anterior larynx that is hard to bring into view
questions.explanation: TMD >9 cm suggests a caudal larynx.

questions.stem: The hyoid-to-thyroid distance is only one fingerbreadth. What airway difficulty does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Less than 2 fingerbreadths suggests an anterior larynx.

questions.stem: A patient cannot flex the neck to the chest or extend at the atlantooccipital joint. How should this affect the airway plan?
options: Low Mallampati class with an easy view
Easy mask ventilation with normal anatomy
Limited range of motion predicting difficult laryngoscopy
Normal range of motion for the patient's age and size
questions.explanation: Limited head and neck ROM is a difficulty predictor.

questions.stem: A highly arched, narrow palate is found despite otherwise normal airway measurements. What does this add to the assessment?
options: Easy intubation with a Mac blade
questions.explanation: A highly arched or narrow palate suggests difficulty.

questions.stem: An edentulous patient has sunken cheeks and a persistent mask leak. What is the most likely reason?
questions.explanation: Edentulous patients have altered facial structure and poor seal.

questions.stem: An elderly patient's mask seal worsens when well-fitting dentures are removed. What is the best approach during BMV?
options: Remove the dentures before mask ventilation
Use a smaller mask so it sits inside the sunken cheeks
Use a smaller mask without dentures
Leave the dentures in for BMV
questions.explanation: Dentures can be left in during BMV if they improve the seal, then removed before laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Mask ventilation remains difficult because an NG tube disrupts the facial seal. Which simple modification may help?
options: Give lidocaine to relax the cords
questions.explanation: NG tube removal may improve the seal.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy yields a Cormack-Lehane grade I view. What does this generally predict?
questions.explanation: Grades I–IIa are generally easier.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy shows neither epiglottis nor glottic structures. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to VL or readjust your technique
Change to a smaller blade and repeat the same attempt
questions.explanation: With a grade IV view, readjust positioning or technique, or move to videolaryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Mallampati III and a thyromental distance of 5 cm are both present. What is the combined implication?
options: Low risk of difficulty with these findings
BMV is difficult but laryngoscopy is not
Mask ventilation is affected but laryngoscopy is not
questions.explanation: Combining predictors increases accuracy.

questions.stem: A prominent upper-incisor overbite is present despite normal neck mobility. Which airway task becomes more concerning?
options: Mask seal is affected but laryngoscopy is not
Easier laryngoscopy from a wider view
questions.explanation: Prominent overbite suggests difficulty.

questions.stem: During the upper lip bite test, the lower incisors can bite the upper lip but remain below the vermilion border. Which class is this?
options: Normal Mallampati with class I view
Lower incisors align but bite below the vermilion border
Lower incisors bite above the vermilion border
questions.explanation: Class B aligns with upper incisors but bites below the vermilion border.

questions.stem: A sternomental distance of 11 cm is measured. What does this suggest?
options: Normal airway with low predicted difficulty
questions.explanation: SMD <12.5 cm is associated with difficulty.

questions.stem: Atlantooccipital extension is limited to 18°. What does this finding predict?
questions.explanation: Extension <23° predicts difficulty.

questions.stem: A neck circumference of 48 cm is measured. Which airway risks increase?
questions.explanation: Neck circumference >43 cm suggests difficulty.

questions.stem: A patient has only 2.5 cm of mouth opening. Which THREE airway maneuvers or devices are directly limited by the restricted oral aperture? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Restricted opening limits blades, SGAs, and ETTs; nasal FIS may work.

questions.stem: A patient with Down syndrome presents for anesthesia. Which paired airway concern is most important to anticipate?
options: Airway obstruction with limited cervical mobility
Increased mouth opening with easier laryngoscopy
Reduced tongue size with improved mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Down syndrome is associated with airway obstruction and cervical issues.

questions.stem: A patient with Pierre Robin sequence presents for anesthesia. Which airway problem should be anticipated?
questions.explanation: Pierre Robin is a congenital cause of obstruction.

questions.stem: Severe hypotension and metabolic acidosis are present before intubation despite normal airway anatomy. Which difficult-airway category applies?
questions.explanation: Severe hypoxia, hypotension, or acidosis create a physiologic difficult airway.

questions.stem: An expanding neck hematoma develops after carotid surgery. Which category of difficult airway does this represent?
questions.explanation: Hematomas are pathophysiologic causes.

questions.stem: Severe facial trauma prevents mouth opening and makes oral access impossible. Which approach should be prepared early?
options: Prepare for surgical airway or cricothyrotomy
Standard DL with a Mac 4 blade and stylet
questions.explanation: Traumatic facial injury may require front-of-neck access.

questions.stem: The airway plan includes a primary technique, backup devices, and front-of-neck rescue readiness. Which algorithm principle does this demonstrate?
options: Avoiding backup plans to save induction time
Planning for primary and alternative strategies
questions.explanation: Algorithms emphasize primary and backup plans.

questions.stem: In the Airway Approach Algorithm, which question specifically addresses aspiration risk?
options: Is the patient at risk of rapid desaturation?
questions.explanation: One question asks whether aspiration risk has been minimized.

questions.stem: Which patient is most likely to benefit from apneic oxygenation because safe-apnea time is expected to be short?
options: A healthy patient with normal FRC
questions.explanation: Obese patients desaturate quickly and benefit most.

questions.stem: Preoxygenation is limited by a poor mask seal in a patient expected to desaturate quickly. Which adjunct can provide additional oxygen during the attempt?
options: Apneic oxygenation with high-flow nasal cannula
Lower FiO2 to reduce absorption atelectasis
Vital capacity breaths through the same mask
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation can help maintain oxygenation during intubation.

questions.stem: A 5'2" woman has an oral ETT secured at 28 cm at the lip. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Deep insertion risks mainstem intubation, usually right.

questions.stem: A 6.0-mm ETT is producing unexpectedly high resistance despite no kink or secretions. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Resistance stays about the same across tube sizes
questions.explanation: Smaller ETTs increase resistance and work of breathing.

questions.stem: An ETT cuff pressure of 10 cmH2O produces an audible leak. What is the best adjustment?
options: Leave the leak, since cuff pressure should stay near zero
Increase to the minimum pressure that stops the leak, under 25 cmH2O
Deflate the cuff and ventilate around it
Increase to 40 cmH2O for a tight seal
questions.explanation: Inflate to the minimum volume that prevents leaks, <25 cmH2O.

questions.stem: Which THREE patients would benefit most from identifying and marking the cricothyroid membrane before induction? (Select 3)
options: Patients with Mallampati I and normal neck
questions.explanation: Mark the membrane in high-risk patients.

questions.stem: After tracheal intubation, which single finding provides the most reliable routine confirmation of placement?
questions.explanation: ETCO2 capnography is most reliable.

questions.stem: Direct laryngoscopy reveals the epiglottis and posterior arytenoid structures but not the full vocal cords. Which view and adjunct best fit this situation?
options: Grade IV; proceed to cric immediately
Grade IIb–III range; use a bougie or BURP
Grade I; pass the tube directly under vision
questions.explanation: Seeing only posterior structures is a poor view; bougie or BURP helps.

questions.stem: With maximal mouth opening and tongue protrusion, only the hard palate is visible. Which Mallampati class is present?
questions.explanation: Class IV shows hard palate only.

questions.stem: Which head-and-neck position best improves direct-laryngoscopy alignment of the airway axes?
options: Head elevated on a pad with head extension (sniffing)
Head flat on the bed in a neutral position
Head elevated on a pad without extension
Head rotated to the side with the neck flexed
questions.explanation: Sniffing position aligns the axes.

questions.stem: After inserting a curved laryngoscope blade along the right side of the mouth, what should occur next?
options: Lift straight up without moving the tongue aside
Rock the blade back on the upper teeth for leverage
Rotate the handle clockwise toward the teeth
Sweep the tongue left and advance to the midline tongue base
questions.explanation: Insert right, sweep tongue left, advance midline, then lift forward at 45°.

questions.stem: During nasotracheal intubation, the tube should travel along the nasal floor beneath which turbinate?
questions.explanation: The tube follows the nasal floor beneath the inferior turbinate.

questions.stem: A lesion is centered in the pharyngeal segment around C5–C6. Which segment is involved?
questions.explanation: The hypopharynx is at C5–C6.

questions.stem: After thyroid surgery, new hoarseness and an ineffective cough develop. Which nerve injury is most likely?
questions.explanation: RLN injury causes hoarseness.

questions.stem: Emergency front-of-neck access is required after failed oxygenation. Which surface landmark is the key target?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane lies between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

questions.stem: A small adult is intubated to 26 cm and left-sided breath sounds disappear. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Left mainstem intubation from a deep tube
questions.explanation: The steeper right bronchus favors right mainstem intubation.

questions.stem: A patient has only two fingerbreadths of mouth opening. What does the 3-3-2 assessment predict?
options: Anterior larynx that is hard to visualize
questions.explanation: Fewer than 3 fingerbreadths suggests inadequate opening.

questions.stem: Which difficult-airway-cart item is used specifically to confirm tracheal tube placement rather than facilitate insertion?
questions.explanation: Confirmation tools include capnography and esophageal detectors.

questions.stem: For awake nasal intubation, which topical agent provides both local anesthesia and vasoconstriction?
questions.explanation: Cocaine provides topical anesthesia and vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: During awake airway preparation, which nerve supplies sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve supplies the anterior tongue.

questions.stem: During a glossopharyngeal block near the tonsillar pillar, why is aspiration before injection essential?
options: It confirms nerve stimulation before injecting
The carotid artery lies close to the injection site
It confirms tracheal placement of the needle
It prevents coughing during the injection
questions.explanation: Avoid intravascular injection near the carotid.

questions.stem: During a superior laryngeal nerve block, which tactile change suggests the needle has crossed the thyrohyoid membrane?
options: A loss of resistance to air in a syringe
questions.explanation: Resistance or a bounce indicates the thyrohyoid membrane.

questions.stem: Cricoid pressure is intended to compress which structure against the cervical vertebrae?
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure compresses the esophagus against the cervical spine.

questions.stem: Which surgical procedure is specifically associated with increased difficult-extubation risk?
questions.explanation: Head and neck surgery increases difficult extubation risk.

questions.stem: Arytenoid dislocation occurs after traumatic intubation. Which clinical consequence is most likely?
questions.explanation: Laryngeal trauma causes hoarseness and possible obstruction.

questions.stem: When capnography is uncertain and direct visualization is desired, which confirmation method is highly sensitive but less practical?
questions.explanation: Seeing tracheal rings with a bronchoscope is sensitive but not always available or practical; capnography is the standard.
